s01.slug: THURSDAY · 7:00 AM · N. DUPRE STREET, THE ATTIC
body: Gray gets to the attic first. It comes in at the gable window past the box fan standing switched off in the frame with its blades still, and spreads along the three mattresses without warming anybody on them. Over Jack’s face the nails come down through the roof deck in their rows. All week the points have beaded in the cold and let go a drop at a time onto whoever slept under them. This morning they are dry.

He says the penance on his knees at the window, with his breath on the glass: the seventh morning. *He summoned the Twelve and began to send them out two by two.* It comes out whole now, without a stumble, down to the oil, and he doesn’t trust that either.

Two houses down somebody has a radio going behind a shut window, a man on WWL reading the traffic at the I-10 split. The RAZR is on the sill where he left it at midnight. The little outside screen says two, both from Burnaby, both from the last minutes he was asleep.

body: Rain, six.
Further down, under them, is the one he opened Wednesday at five past two in the morning. He goes back up to the moon.

He can see her sending it: the lot at the end of a night shoot with the big lights coming down one bank at a time, a parka over whatever wardrobe had her in, her thumbs going on the white phone in the door of the trailer, so pleased with Dutch she couldn’t wait until she was lying down to tell somebody. Out the gable window the sky over Mid-City is low and gray and has nothing in it, no moon, real or rented. A pigeon sits on somebody’s TV antenna, facing the wrong way. Jack stands at the window in his socks with the phone open, smiling at a balloon over Burnaby he has never seen, and at Dutch, whom he never will.
“Day four,” Theo says into the pillow.

He is face-down on the middle mattress in a Marisol crew sweatshirt, one arm hanging off the edge onto the boards with the hand open, palm up, in the place where his phone used to sleep. It has been zipped into the inside pocket of Kevin’s windbreaker since Monday, at his own request, on the road out of the airport in Kenner, and Theo has been taking it hard.

By the hatch Kevin sits cross-legged on his sleeping bag, dressed, with a ziplock bag open in his lap. He is counting red envelopes out of it onto his knee, red paper printed in gold, a stack about the thickness of a deck of cards, and his lips move with the count.
“He’s asked for it in his sleep,” Kevin says, still counting. “Twice. Once in French.”
“I don’t speak French,” Theo says, into the pillow.
“You do asleep.”
“What did I say?”
“I don’t speak French.”

Kevin looks up from the envelopes and finds Jack looking at them. He taps the stack even on his knee, slides it back into the ziplock, runs the zipper shut along its track with his thumb, puts the bag down inside his sleeping bag, and starts on his shoes.
The phone is still open in Jack’s hand, with Dutch’s moon on it.

s02.slug: THURSDAY · 7:50 AM · OUR LADY OF THE HOLY ROSARY, ESPLANADE AVENUE — LOURDES
body: At a quarter past seven Mémère is waiting at the foot of the attic ladder, dressed and pinned, in a navy coat with a cameo at the throat and her purse hooked over her wrist, and Lena beside her in a jean jacket with her hair still wet. When Jack comes down the last rungs, Mémère holds one arm out to Lena, who takes it, and the other arm out to the empty air on her other side, and looks at Jack until he understands.
“*Toi*,” she says. “*L’autre bras.*”

So they walk the four blocks to Esplanade at her pace, one of them on either side of her. She isn’t light on an arm. At every curb her weight comes off Lena and onto Jack going down, and off Jack and onto Lena coming up, and halfway across one street she stops all three of them to look both ways herself, because she has seen how they drive.

Holy Rosary on a Thursday morning holds sixty people, most of them old, spread through the front half of the nave in their coats. The light comes in at the east windows thin and yellow and lies across the pews in long panes with the dust turning in them. Hébert is in white for Our Lady. A nurse in Touro scrubs, with her badge clipped on and a rosary wound through her fingers, slips into the last pew on her way in to her shift. Mémère takes the Gospel side, the family’s side, and sits down between the two of them as if she had built the pew for the purpose.
The organ starts the old Lourdes hymn, and voices that have been singing it since Eisenhower take it each at its own speed and come in together on the Aves.

Hébert reads the Gospel himself, short and dry. A woman who isn’t one of His people falls at Christ’s feet for her daughter, and He tells her the children get fed first, it isn’t right to throw their bread to the dogs, and she doesn’t get up. Hébert gives her answer its full weight. “*Lord, even the dogs under the table eat the children’s scraps.*”
On the far side of her grandmother, not moving her lips, Lena says, “Aints would like a word with the Gospel.”

The laugh comes up in Jack from somewhere under the kneeler and gets as far as his nose. He turns it into a cough, and the cough into a long, devout study of the hymnal rack, and Mémère, without turning her head, puts one sharp elbow into his arm. Past her, Lena’s face is a holy card. Whatever is going on behind her teeth stays there.

The homily is four minutes, without notes. Hébert stands at the front of the sanctuary, a small brown old man with his hands folded on his stomach. “She argued with Him,” he says, “and she won. He lets you. I think He likes it.” He looks out over the sixty of them. “There are people in this parish who have been arguing with Him for eighty-eight years. They know who they are. Some of them are coming up for the oil this morning, and they’ll argue with me on the way.”

After the homily the old and the sick of the parish come up. A man pushing his own walker. A woman with an oxygen line looped over her ears and her son at her elbow. A girl younger than Jack in a Saints beanie with no hair under it, holding her mother’s hand. Mémère rises on Jack’s arm. He walks her up the aisle to the altar step, and at the step she lets go of him and goes up the rest of the way alone.

Hébert lays his hands on her head first, without a word. He wets his thumb in the oil stock and draws the cross on her forehead. “*Through this holy anointing may the Lord in his love and mercy help you with the grace of the Holy Spirit.*” Mémère says *Amen* like a woman shutting a gate. He takes her hands and turns them palm up, one and then the other, and crosses them with the oil. “*May the Lord who frees you from sin save you and raise you up.*” “*Amen.*” Then he bends to her and says something in French too low for the pews, and whatever she says back makes the altar server bite his lip.

Jack, at the end of the pew where she left him, watches the old man’s thumb go into the oil and come out shining and go to the next forehead, and the next, and his eyes sting, and he keeps them on it.
Mémère comes back down the step to his arm with her palms held a little open in front of her, as if she were carrying water.

When the last of the old people have gone out on their walkers and the server is putting out the altar candles, she steers the two of them, one on each arm, down the side aisle to the grotto. It’s a niche in the wall: rock made of plaster and painted gray and green, Our Lady standing up in it in white with a blue sash and her eyes raised, and Bernadette kneeling at the foot in a brown dress with her hands together. In front of them stands an iron rack of vigil lights in red glass, three rows, a third of them burning. A coin box. A coffee can of long wooden matches.
Mémère puts a dollar in the box, folded small, takes a match, and lights one in the top row. She stands with the match burning down in her fingers and speaks to the statue in French.
“*Je ne vous promets pas de vous rendre heureuse en ce monde, mais dans l’autre.*”

All week Lena has let half her grandmother’s French go past Jack untranslated, or translated it into whatever suited her. This one she gives him word for word. She says it with her eyes on the candles. “I do not promise to make you happy in this world. But in the other.”

body: Mémère shakes out the match. She turns to Jack and looks at him through the bottoms of her bifocals, close, as she reads the obituaries.
“*Et toi. Tu pries pour qui?*”
Lena doesn’t translate it. She doesn’t have to.

response: “My brother,” Jack says.

“*Bon.*” Mémère takes a fresh match out of the coffee can and puts it in his hand. He strikes it on the side of the box and lights a candle in the second row, and the flame catches and stands up straight in the red glass. In Trumbull they’ll have done the morning count by now.
Lena takes the match out of his fingers before it has burned down and lights hers off his flame, and shakes it out.

choices.key: On the feast of Lourdes, at the grotto in Holy Rosary, Mémère asked who you light a candle for. A girl in Canada, you told her. Pray for her, she said.
response: “A girl in Canada,” Jack says.
Lena’s hands are on the iron rail in front of the candles. They stay there. Mémère looks at him, and then at her granddaughter, for a long Breaux Bridge second, and back at him.
“*Bon.*” She puts a match in his hand. “*Prie pour elle.*”

He lights one in the second row for Skye, for Mary Kate, asleep in her coat in Burnaby. Lena takes the match out of his fingers while it is still burning and lights the next candle off his, and doesn’t say for whom.

choices.key: On the feast of Lourdes, at the grotto in Holy Rosary, Mémère asked who you light a candle for. Everybody in her house, you told her. She gave you two matches.
response: “Everybody in your house, Madame.”
“*Tout le monde?*”
“*Tout le monde.*”

Mémère starts counting on her fingers: *Antoine*, *Céleste*, Luc, Tess and Beau and the baby, Rémy, the twins. She runs out of fingers somewhere around Clovis and the dog, looks at her hands, gives up, and gives him two matches. Lena lights hers off his second candle.

s02a.slug: THURSDAY · 8:35 AM · HOLY ROSARY, THE VESTIBULE — AND ESPLANADE
body: In the vestibule, on a nail by the holy-water font, a typed card hangs in a dime-store frame with the gilt worn off its corners.

body.title: Framed by the holy water, Holy Rosary vestibule
body.text:
CONFESSIONS
SATURDAY · 3:00–4:00 P.M.
FR. HÉBERT

body: He reads it.

Hébert is at the front doors in a black overcoat thrown on over his alb, shaking the hand of everybody who goes out into the wind. When Jack comes by with Mémère on his arm the old priest’s eyes go over him, quick and dry, and he takes Jack’s hand in both of his.
“*Le garçon de l’Ohio*,” he says.
He turns to Mémère. “Odile. You’re glowing. It’s the oil.”
She slaps his hand away, not hard, and lets him kiss her cheek.

Esplanade is oaks and old houses with their Carnival flags out, purple and green and gold, cracking on their poles in the wind off the bayou. They take her home the four blocks at her pace, her hands on their arms again. Where she holds his sleeve he can smell it coming off her palms in the cold, faint and green: olive oil, and something older under it. Halfway home Mémère says something to Lena across him, short, with a nod at his middle. “*Il est bon, celui-là. Mais trop maigre.*”
“She says you need feeding,” Lena says.

s03.slug: THURSDAY · 10:20 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH
body: The porch is in shade. The swing hangs crooked on its chains, lower on the street side, and moves when he does. Jack sits in it with the RAZR on the slat beside him and his wallet open on his knee. Across Dupre Street a man in a Saints toboggan is wrestling a stepladder down off his porch with a padlock and a length of chain hung over his shoulder, and the woman in the doorway behind him is telling him where.
Seventy-one dollars: three twenties, a ten, and a one gone soft as cloth. Behind them in the bill fold, folded small, his father’s note: IT’S ALLOWED.
Sunday is Valentine’s Day. She’s on a lot in Burnaby with a goose.

It has been on his mind since Monday, in the coffee aisle, with the rice on his shoulder. He counts the money again. It’s still seventy-one. The phone lies on the slat with its little screen dark, and inside it the last thing from her is still the moon.
The screen door goes on its spring, and Kevin comes out with the Odyssey’s keys in one hand and a bank envelope in the other, already folded down the middle to fit his windbreaker.
“Bank,” he says. “New bills. For the envelopes. It has to be new bills, it’s a whole thing.” He holds up the keys. “Going downtown. Anybody needs anything, speak now.”
Behind him comes Lena, in the Broussard’s Seafood sweatshirt that’s older than the twins, with her hair dry now and up, and her father’s second ring of keys hooked on one finger.
“Register till two,” she says, to both of them.
“You want a ride?” Kevin says.
“It’s a mile, Kevin. I’ve walked it since I was six.”
She looks at the wallet open on his knee, and at the phone on the swing beside it, and doesn’t ask. The keys go round her finger and stop.

choices.text: “Lena. Is there a florist near the market?”
response: “Miss Dot,” she says, before he has got to the end of it. “Next door to us. She did Tess’s wedding.” She goes down the steps ahead of him and holds the gate open with her hip, and waits, with the keys going.

s03b.slug: THURSDAY · 11:00 AM · CANAL STREET → A BOOKSHOP ON DECATUR STREET
body: The bank on Canal is an old one, with a marble floor worn into a path from the door to the tellers and brass grilles over the windows gone brown. Kevin slides his envelope under the glass.
“New bills, please. As new as you’ve got.” He thinks about it. “And two-dollar bills, if you have any.” The teller looks at him. “Lucky,” Kevin explains. “It’s — it’s very specific.”

The teller is about Celeste’s age, with her glasses on a beaded chain and a name tag that says HUONG. She looks at the envelope, and at him, and opens a drawer and comes up with a strap of twos so new they stick together. “*Chúc mừng năm mới*,” she says. Three days early.

Kevin answers her in Vietnamese. He gets a good way into the sentence before it goes out from under him, and he stands there with his mouth open on a word that isn’t coming, and the teller waits him out, smiling, and supplies it. Kevin laughs at himself with his forehead nearly on the counter.
“My grandmother just felt that,” he tells Jack. “In San Jose.”

The teller counts the twos out twice and bands them, and Kevin puts them in the bank envelope with the rest and folds it down the middle, and holds it a moment between his palms before it goes inside his windbreaker.
Out on the sidewalk, Jack says, “Lucky how?”
“Lucky like it’s lucky,” Kevin says. “You don’t ask a horseshoe how.”

They leave the Odyssey at a meter and walk down into the Quarter. The river is a block over, and the wind brings it up Decatur Street: mud, diesel, the sugar off a praline shop. At eleven in the morning a bar has its door propped open with a mop bucket and a bartender cutting limes in the dark behind it, and out of the dark comes a piano, a record of one, rolling and drunk-sounding and landing every note anyway, and a man singing over it like he has been up all night and regrets none of it. Kevin slows down to hear it. So does a mule standing in its harness at the curb with a carriage behind it and a plastic flower over one ear.

The bookshop is three floors in an old Creole building, narrow as a hallway, with shelves somebody built by hand going up the stairwell walls. A gray cat sleeps on the fourth stair with its paws folded under, and everybody going up steps over it. At the register a man in a cardigan reads a paperback through a magnifying glass the size of a saucer and lets the bell over the door ring. Kevin peels off toward the foreign languages on the ground floor. Jack steps over the cat and goes up, and the stairs say something about it under every foot.

He knows what he wants before he finds it. Literature is at the back of the second floor, under a window painted shut, and the O’Connors are on the bottom shelf between O’Brien and O’Hara. Two copies of *A Good Man Is Hard to Find*, which he doesn’t need: she has hers, with her margins in it. *The Habit of Being*, which he leaves where it is; somebody read the peacock letters out of that one in a van once. And at the end of the row, thin, in a library binding gone soft at the corners, *Mystery and Manners*.

Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1969. DISCARD stamped across the empty card pocket inside the back cover. Somebody read it before him with a pencil, a light, argumentative pencil that underlines and puts question marks in the margins and once, beside a paragraph about the Church, writes *no*. The price is on the flyleaf in the shop’s own hand: $18.

body.else: Near the back is the essay where O’Connor, talking to a room of college students about her own story, says what he said to her that night in his own words: that the grandmother’s gesture is where grace comes in.

body: He sits down on the floor in the aisle with his back to Faulkner and turns to it. The pencil has been there before him too: two lines down the margin beside the passage, and a question mark, and then, crowded in after the question mark, a check. O’Connor is talking to a room full of college students who have decided the grandmother is the villain of the piece, and she tells them, more patiently than he would have, that the old lady at the end finally sees she is responsible for the man in front of her, that she is kin to him, down where the mystery is that she has been chattering about since Atlanta.

Eighteen dollars out of seventy-one. He gets up off the floor with it.
Downstairs, Kevin has found a Vietnamese-English phrasebook from 1975 with a cracked spine and a water stain shaped like Florida, and he pays the man a dollar for it.
“So I can bluff better on Sunday,” he tells Jack. He turns it over and reads the back. “Page forty-one is how to tell a woman her soup is excellent. That’s going to come up.”

At the register Jack opens *Mystery and Manners* on the counter and borrows the shop’s pen, a ballpoint on a bead chain screwed down to the wood. He turns his shoulder to Kevin, who has the phrasebook open to a chapter on bargaining, and writes *Mary Kate* at the top of the flyleaf, where only she is going to see it.

body: The FedEx on Canal has a line of four, a dusty ficus, and a clerk with a Saints lanyard and a pencil behind each ear. The man ahead of them is mailing two king cakes to Houston in a box built for a microwave. “My daughter,” he tells the line, without being asked. “They sell them out there. She says they taste like a Sunday at the mall.” Kevin reads the packing-tape display as if it were a menu.

Jack fills out the International Priority form at the counter by the window. Before it goes in the box he wraps the book in a sports page somebody left on the counter, Wednesday’s, with the parade on it, the trophy going down St. Charles in the confetti, so that something of the city goes with it. Then into a padded box about the size of a cigar box, and the flaps down, and the tape. He knows the hotel in Burnaby from her calls, the street and the room number she always says like the last line of a joke, and he prints it all out in block letters and her name on the line for the recipient. On the customs line, under contents, he writes BOOK, USED. Under value he writes 18.00. It’s the right number, and it looks wrong on the form, and he leaves it.
The clerk weighs it and runs the form through her fingers. “Friday by end of day,” she says. “Maybe Saturday. Customs.”

Jack takes the clerk’s Sharpie off the counter and writes SUNDAY across the top of the box in capitals, big enough to read from behind a hotel desk. The clerk watches him do it and doesn’t say anything about the regulations. Behind them, the king-cake man says, “Well, all *right*,” to the line in general.
The register says sixty-six forty.

He has fifty-three dollars. He’s laying it out on the counter, two twenties and a ten and three ones, and is about to count it again when Kevin reaches past him and puts down a ten and two of the new two-dollar bills off the strap, so new they click against each other.
“It’s a loan,” Kevin says. “I’ll invoice you.”

The clerk gives Jack sixty cents back. Jack gives it to Kevin, who puts it in the pocket of his windbreaker without comment and zips the pocket. The box goes into a canvas cart behind the counter with a cartload of other boxes going everywhere else, and SUNDAY is the last thing Jack can see of it, upside down.

Outside, Canal Street goes by in both directions: a bus, the red streetcar with its bell going, a man with a pole hung with beads selling them to the cars at the light. In front of one of the big hotels a crew in orange vests is bolting bleachers together for the weekend, and the sound of the wrenches comes across the neutral ground in the wind. Kevin stands at the edge of the curb with his hands in his windbreaker, looking at the traffic.
“You mean it,” Kevin says.
“Yeah.”
“Good. People should get to.”
He steps off the curb to the meter, reads it, and feeds it a quarter.
The little window turns up an hour. Kevin pats it on the head.

s03f.slug: THURSDAY · 10:40 AM · BANKS STREET — MISS DOT’S
s03f.music: Irma Thomas — “Time Is on My Side”
body: Lena walks him down Dupre and across Canal to Banks Street, a mile of it, with her keys going round her finger and the sidewalk heaving up in slabs over the oak roots, so that you walk it like a deck in weather. She doesn’t say a word about where he’s going or why. She tells him about Mr. Dupuy.

“He’s going to call at eleven,” she says, “with a basket he’s going to tell me is number ones. And it’s going to be number ones on top, like a church bake sale, and underneath it’s going to be whatever his nephew found. It’s the Thursday before Endymion and he thinks everybody’s too busy to dig.” She steps over a root without looking at it. “I am going to dig.”
“You could send them back,” Jack says.

“Then I don’t have crabs, and he has a story. The Broussard girl who sent his crabs back, Tony’s, the mouthy one. He tells it at the Knights of Columbus fish fry every Friday in Lent till one of us is dead.” Her keys go round. “No, sir. I dig, I pay him twos for the bottom and ones for the ones, and he thanks me. And then he tells *that* story, which is a better story, and everybody at the fish fry is on my side.”
Miss Dot’s is a narrow shopfront next door to the market, with a striped awning and buckets of red roses crowding the window glass from the inside.
“Tell her you’re with us,” Lena says, and goes on next door, and the market’s bell rings behind her.

Miss Dot’s smells of cold water and cut stems and fern. There are roses everywhere, in buckets on the floor, on the counter, on two kitchen chairs pushed against the wall, red on red; and on a chalkboard by the register somebody has written ROSES $55 DOZ, and crossed out the 55, and written 65 over it, and left room. The cooler hums along the back wall. On top of it a plastic Zenith radio is playing something slow and sure of itself, a woman from a long time ago taking all the time she likes.

Miss Dot comes out of the back drying her hands on her apron: seventies, small, in a lavender cardigan buttoned to the neck with a rhinestone fleur-de-lis pinned over her heart, and her hair done up high and set hard enough to stand a parade. On the wall behind the register are decades of brides in drugstore frames. Near the top, Tess in white, laughing, with a bouquet the size of a hubcap, and over her shoulder, in a row of bridesmaids with their chins up, Lena.
“Baby,” she says, which is hello.
“I need to send flowers,” Jack says. “Violets.”
She waits.
“White ones,” he says. “In a pot. To Canada.”
Miss Dot puts her towel down on the counter.
“In February,” she says.
“Yes ma’am.”

“Violets. White. In a *pot*. To *Canada*.” She says each one slower than the last. “Baby, I have been in this shop forty years. I did a casket spray in the shape of the Superdome in 1987 and it stood up in the rain at Lake Lawn. I did eight hundred carnations in purple and gold for a bishop’s jubilee. I have never in forty years been asked for violets in February in a pot to Canada.”
She looks at him over her glasses, and he can see the moment it stops being an insult and starts being a dare. She takes a pencil out of her hair.
“Where in Canada.”
“Burnaby. Outside Vancouver. It’s a film lot. She’s in a trailer.”
“Course she is,” Miss Dot says, and heaves a wire-service book as thick as a phone book up onto the counter, and licks her thumb.

While she pages she asks him things, in the order she asks everybody. The girl’s name. Skye. “Like the weather,” Miss Dot says, and writes it. Is she pretty. Yes ma’am. Is she Catholic. He thinks about how to answer that honestly, and says she’s been to Mass with him, and Miss Dot says, “Well, that’s a start, baby,” and licks her thumb again.
“She know where you are? Down here?”
“Yes ma’am. She told me to come.”
Miss Dot looks at him over the pencil, and then out her front window at Banks Street, where Lena went by with her keys ten minutes ago. “Hm,” she says.

Violets, because of a hat: the grandmother’s navy straw sailor with white violets on the brim, put on for the drive so that anybody who found her dead on the highway would know she was a lady, the detail a girl on a window seat in Montecito loved best and read backwards, as a performer’s last line.
“You with somebody?” Miss Dot says, finding her page.
“I’m — Lena said to tell you I’m with them. The Broussards.”
Miss Dot looks up. “Tony’s?”
“Yes ma’am.”

“Well, why didn’t you say so.” She writes a number on her pad and draws a line through the number under it, the February one. “I’ve known Antoine Broussard thirty years. He sold my husband the crawfish for every Good Friday we had. You pay me the wire and the pot, baby, and you don’t pay me February.” She turns the pad so he can read it. It comes to thirty-one dollars, and he puts two twenties on the counter before she can change her mind, and she makes his change out of a cigar box and pats his hand when she gives it to him.

She dials Canada on a beige wall phone with a cord that reaches every corner of the shop. While it rings she explains how this goes: the lady up there writes out the card on her end, in her own hand. Miss Dot reads it to her. So he is going to tell Miss Dot what it says, and Miss Dot is going to tell Canada.

Burnaby answers, and Miss Dot puts on her best voice, which is the one she was born with turned up for company. “Good morning, darling, this is Dot Pellerin at Miss Dot’s on Banks Street in New Orleans, Louisiana, and I have got a puzzle for you.”
The lady in Burnaby has white violets. African ones, in clay. Miss Dot covers the receiver with her palm. “African,” she reports. “It’s what the Lord left her in February.”
“That’s fine,” Jack says. “White?”

“White,” Miss Dot tells Canada. “And it’s going to a *trailer*, darling, on a movie lot, and you put it in her hands yourself. You don’t leave it with some boy in a headset.” She covers the receiver again. “When?”
“Friday night,” Jack says. “Late as they’ll go. She works nights.”

“Friday night, late as you go,” Miss Dot tells Canada. “She works nights.” There is an opinion in it about girls who work nights on movie lots, and she keeps the rest of it, for Tony’s sake, to herself.

She turns to Jack with the pencil up and the receiver tucked under her chin. “Who’s it from, baby, and what’s it say?” He understands that she is going to read his card down a telephone line to a stranger in British Columbia, slowly, among sixty dozen roses, and that there is no other way on earth for this to happen. He would like, very much, to be any man in Louisiana but the one at this counter.

s03g.slug: THURSDAY · 11:40 AM → 1:10 PM · BROUSSARD’S SEAFOOD, BANKS STREET
body: Next door the market’s bell is going steady, Banks Street coming in for the weekend, and the case is half empty already. Tony sees him through the front glass and points with his chin at the white rubber boots standing by the walk-in.

body.text: “You know ice,” Tony says, and that’s the interview.
body.else: “Ohio. Ice.” Tony shows him how it goes in one sentence, high at the back and running down to the glass so the melt finds the drain, and leaves him to it.

body: So he gives the hour to the ice, in Tony’s spare boots and a rubber apron. The crabs go into the bushel baskets on the floor by size, blue and furious and reaching for him through the slats. The redfish go on the bed in a row with their eyes clear, the big ones forward. The melt runs down the pitch of the concrete to the drain in the middle of the floor. At the oyster bench under the front window Mr. Alcide opens his dozens for the lunch trade, singing along in French with the red radio, and lifts his knife to Jack in greeting, an old hand to a new one. When Tony comes down the case with a pan he moves the big ones to the front with the side of his hand, and goes back to the scale.

Mr. Dupuy calls at ten to twelve. Lena takes the wall phone the length of the case on its cord, crouches over the basket on the floor, and digs. Two layers down she comes up with a crab the size of a coaster and holds it up for the market to see, though Mr. Dupuy, wherever he is, can’t see it. “Mr. Dupuy, I am holding your nephew’s idea of a number one, and it is looking at me with *pity*.” After that it goes as she said it would: twos for the bottom, ones for the ones, and Mr. Dupuy, somewhere down in Lafitte, thanking her.

At one Miss Earline comes in, in her plastic rain bonnet with the Saints scarf tied over it, for a pound of shrimp and the news. She looks down the case at Jack, who is banking ice into the hole the lunch rush has made in it.
“Still here,” Miss Earline says.
“Yes ma’am.”

She accepts this. Lena comes down behind the case for a lemon to go in the bag with the shrimp, and moves Jack out of her way with a hand on his back — the lemons are behind him — as she would move a chair in her own kitchen, without breaking off what she is telling Miss Earline about Endymion. Miss Earline takes her shrimp and her lemon and her news and goes.

In the lull after the door shuts behind her, Lena breaks a roll of quarters on the edge of the drawer and lets them run into their slot, and says, with her eyes on the quarters, “Miss Dot says violets. In February.”
“She’ll know why,” Jack says.
The last of the quarters go in.
“…Good.”
She bumps the drawer shut with her hip and turns to the next one in line, a man in a Hornets jacket who wants two dozen and to know where everybody’s putting their ladders.

s04.slug: THURSDAY · 5:30 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — SNOW IN DALLAS
body: Jack comes in by the back steps to a kitchen that is already full, with the windows steamed and the Magic Chef going and everybody sitting in the wrong chair. Theo, phoneless, has the parade schedule out of the *Picayune* open on the oilcloth and is reading it with one finger, like scripture. Margot is on the piano bench under the window with Durkheim on her knee. Celeste, home from Touro in her scrubs still, has her back to all of them at the stove, and the kitchen smells of onions going brown.

On the counter by the stove Celeste’s little television has WWL on, and WWL has Dallas: a map of North Texas gone white from the Red River down, and then a reporter in a parka on an overpass, with the snow going past him sideways and the traffic stopped under him in both directions with its headlights on. FLIGHTS CANCELED, says the crawl along the bottom of the screen.
Laney is at the counter in Tony’s Saints sweatshirt, which comes to her knees, with her elbows on the Formica and her face close to the screen.
“Mama,” Laney says to the television, the way you’d say a hurricane’s name.

The pink BlackBerry on the counter beside her lights up and starts to turn in a slow circle on its own buzzing. Laney grabs it, gets it upside down, hits something, and Tammy Price comes out of it on speaker, at full pageant, into the kitchen.

“Delaney Rose, are you *watching* this? Are you watching what they are doing to Dallas? The lights have gone off twice. The Mercedes is a *drift*, Delaney Rose, it is a *shape* in the driveway, the neighbor boy came over with a shovel and couldn’t find it. The Henderson boys are sledding down Beverly Drive on cafeteria trays, *Beverly Drive*, Delaney Rose, like it’s Colorado. And they have canceled my flight. *Canceled* it. I had a seat. I had a seat tomorrow morning, and a room on St. Charles, and a dress for the parade, and I had not breathed a syllable of it to you, because I was going to be a *surprise*, Delaney Rose.”
Laney puts both hands over her face. She laughs into them, and her shoulders go, and she can’t do that holding a phone, so she sets it face-up on the counter and leaves it on speaker on purpose.
“This is not what we pay Texas for,” Tammy tells the kitchen. “I have lived in this state forty-six years and I have never asked it for one thing. Is somebody down there feeding my child?”
At the stove Celeste listens to all of it, and stirs.

Tammy doesn’t hang up easily. Laney has to promise to wear a coat to the parades and to send pictures and to stop carrying on, honey, it’s only snow, and Tammy says *I love you, Delaney Rose* three times on the way out, the last one already half into the dial tone.
Laney stands in the middle of the kitchen in Tony’s sweatshirt with the dead phone in her hand, and turns all the way around so that she has faced every one of them.

“Nobody,” she says, “is to do *anything*. For my birthday. Not one thing. No cake, no song, no *card*. I will *know*. And if one person under this roof so much as *hums* at me, I will find out, and I will thank you *so* graciously, in front of God and Miss Celeste, and you will never sleep again.”
At the table Theo puts his hand over his heart. “Nothing,” he says. “We are *experts* in nothing, Mrs. Broussard.”
“Respectfully,” says Kevin, from the end of the table, where he is highlighting the parade schedule over Theo’s shoulder in three colors, “it’s two holidays, a parade and the Lunar New Year.”
“Then nobody do *any* of them.”
Margot turns a page of Durkheim. “Noted.”
Mémère is in the hall doorway in her housecoat with her rosary in her hand. “*Qu’est-ce qu’elle a dit?*”
And Lena, just in at the back door from the market with the cold still on her and her father’s keys still hooked on her finger: “*Rien*, Mémère.”
Laney looks at Lena in the door with the keys on her finger, and at Jack, and at Lena again, and says it louder. “Not *one* thing.” At the table Theo has both hands over his face.
Lena drops her keys on the counter, crosses the kitchen, takes Laney’s face in both hands, and wipes under each of her eyes with her thumbs, one side and then the other, and lets her go.

Celeste says nothing at all. She lays her spoon across the pot, takes the light bill off the top of the refrigerator, turns it over, writes something on the back of it with the pencil from the junk drawer, and puts it back face-down under the Saints magnet.
Laney comes past Jack on her way to the hall, close enough that only he can hear it, with her eyes on the doorway.
“That means you, Ohio.”

response: “Nothing,” Jack says. “I promise.”
Laney stops in the doorway and looks back at him a long second, in Tony’s sweatshirt to her knees.
“See that you don’t,” she says, and goes down the hall past Mémère, who pats her on the arm going by and looks back at the kitchen over her shoulder for an explanation, and doesn’t get one.

choices.text: “I’ll do nothing so hard you’ll feel it.”
response: “I’ll do nothing so hard you’ll feel it.”
“Don’t you *dare* feel it at me, Ohio.” She points at him from the doorway until she is sure it has gone in.
Behind Jack the refrigerator door opens, and Theo goes into it up to the shoulders and stays there, looking very hard for something that isn’t in it.
Jack says nothing.
Laney points at him anyway, from the doorway, one pink fingernail with all of Highland Park behind it. “*Good.*”
At the stove Celeste goes on stirring, and the light bill stays under its magnet.

s05.slug: THURSDAY · 9:40 PM · THE KITCHEN TABLE — FOUR THOUSAND WORDS
body: The house has gone down to its night noises. Through two doors, from the front room, EWTN is saying a litany to Mémère on the daybed in a nun’s patient voice, and out on the porch the swing chain complains under a weight that can only be Tony’s. The bulb over the table makes its yellow room. Behind Jack the Magic Chef is still ticking off the heat of supper, small and dry, a fingernail on a pie tin.

Two yellow legal pads lie on the oilcloth. Four thousand words each, due the Monday they’re back. Hers says PENANCE IN A BAG across the top, underlined, and is on its sixth page; she has Jonah on page three and her mother’s sewing scissors in the second paragraph and the cows of Nineveh wherever she can fit them. His says THE SECOND LINE, and under it is one sentence.

body.text: Under his pad lies Hale’s *Moviegoer*, its spine broken open at Carnival and Hale’s pencil quarreling down every margin, with the print still in the back of it, face-down.
Under his pad lies Hale’s *Moviegoer*, its spine broken open at Carnival and Hale’s pencil quarreling down every margin.

body: He writes a second sentence and crosses it out, and writes it again, worse, and crosses that out too. Lena sits across the corner of the table from him with her hair up in a knot that has a pencil through it and is coming down anyway, one knee up against the edge and her pen going in a hand that leans forward like it’s walking into weather. She reads his sentence upside down without stopping hers.

body.text: “You’ve been in one,” she says. “Once. You were holding an umbrella that wasn’t yours.”
body.else: “You can’t write about a second line you’ve never been in,” she says.

body: “I’ve got till the twenty-second.”

“Mm.” Her pen goes to the end of its line and starts the next one. “Mine’s got Jonah, and the cows, and a grocery sack, and my mother’s sewing scissors, and Hale is going to write *this is a sermon* across the top in red, and he’s going to be right, and I’m going to get an A on it anyway, because it’s a *good* sermon.”
In the front room the nun has got to the Divine Praises, and Mémère is answering her just behind, in French.

body.text: Half a page later, still writing: “Where’d y’all go this morning? You and Kevin.”
“The bank. And FedEx.”
The pen crosses a *t*. “…Valentine’s.”
“Yes.”
“Good,” Lena says, and her pen doesn’t stop.
A minute in, with her eyes on her own page, she says, “White?”
“White.”
She writes a sentence. He watches her get it across the page from margin to margin, and then draw one straight line through it, and start the next.

body: He gets two more sentences out of himself and is into a third when her hand comes across the corner of the table and takes the pen out of his fingers. It’s a black Bic, the end chewed flat. She turns his pad a few degrees toward her with the side of her wrist, and on the fourth line, where he has the city on Canal Street refusing to be *embarased* by its own joy, she puts in the r he left out, and the s while she’s down there.
“Two r’s,” Lena says. “Two s’s. It’s a word that’s ashamed of itself, so it overdoes everything.”

She doesn’t give the pen back. She goes on with her own paragraph in it, Nineveh in his black ink. Somewhere in the last page her bare foot has found the rung of his chair and hooked itself over it, the heel against the wood by his ankle, and it moves when she crosses a word out, and settles when she doesn’t.

When she’s finished her sentence she turns his pad the rest of the way round and reads his best one aloud, in the Oxford she keeps for Hale: “*On the Tuesday after the Super Bowl the city came down Canal Street behind a silver trophy the way a parish walks behind its saint, and nobody had to tell anybody where to stand.*” She lets the pen point at him across the oilcloth. “‘*Nothing about football*,’ Mr. Costigan.”
He reaches over to turn to the next page, where the sentences get worse, and her hand comes down flat on the pad and keeps it there.

response: He takes his hand back. She turns the page herself and reads it, all of it, down to where he quit in the middle of a word, her mouth moving a little on the part about the curb: that he has stood at the edge of every crowd in this city for six days with his hands in his coat, watching it walk away down the street behind a horn.
She turns the pad back round to him and lines it up with the edge of the table.
“That’s the true one,” Lena says. “Keep that one.”
She goes back to her cows, with his pen.

choices.text: “Hale’s going to take points off for the pen.”
response: Lena snorts, with her head going back, and from the front room Mémère asks the litany something in French and gets no answer.
“Then he can take it up with me,” she says. She caps his pen and puts it behind her ear, into her hair, and finishes Nineveh with her own.

Hers is lying by her pad: a blue felt-tip with TOURO INFIRMARY down the barrel in white, the kind her mother brings home by the fistful in her scrub pockets. He picks it up and uncaps it. She watches him do it and says nothing.
It writes wetter than his, and leans when he leans on it. He finds the end of the sentence about Canal Street with it, and the one after. Neither pen goes back.

s06.slug: FRIDAY · 9:30 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE SIDE YARD — THE LADDER
body: Tony’s transistor sits on the upturned boil pot in the middle of the side yard with its antenna up, and WWL is taking calls about ladders. A man in Metairie believes chaining a ladder to the neutral ground on a Thursday ought to be against the law. A woman in Gentilly believes the man in Metairie ought to be against the law. Tony, down on one knee at a sawhorse with a pencil behind his ear, tells the radio that Thursday is late.

Across the sawhorses lies the twins’ ladder: a six-foot wooden stepladder freckled with the paint of every job Tony has ever done for nothing, with a plywood box bolted to the top where the paint shelf used to be — a seat for two, with sides, and a bar across the front for leaning out over. Every year since the twins were four he has taken the box off after Mardi Gras and built a new one before Endymion. This year it’s gold, out of the same can as the bags. Clovis is at the other sawhorse sanding a corner by hand with his coffee in a Saints mug by his boot, and under the picnic table Aints III lies in a quilted coat with snaps down the belly, black and gold, with the face of a lineman who has been asked to wear it.
Jack comes down the back steps with his own coffee.
“Ohio.” Tony holds a yellow drill up over his shoulder. “You know a drill?”
“I know a drill.”

“Endymion’s ours,” Tony says, as if Jack had asked him why a man builds the same ladder twice. “Rex, that’s the city’s. Zulu’s Zulu’s. Bacchus got Brees this year, fine, God bless him, that’s Uptown. Endymion comes down Orleans Avenue.” He points the screwdriver up Dupre Street at Orleans and at all of Mid-City behind it. “Ours.”

The ladders have been out on the Orleans Avenue neutral ground since yesterday, chained to a light pole in a thicket of other families’ ladders, with Clovis’s padlock and Tony’s. “Brass one’s mine,” Clovis says.
Tony shows him the four holes with a fat thumb, and Jack sets the first screw and drives it, and Tony listens to the drill with his head on one side.

body.text: “Celeste mailed your daddy’s paper this morning,” Tony says, holding the next screw up for him. “Carrollton post office. Tuesday, they said. God willing.”

Behind them on the clothesline, between two of Celeste’s sheets, the bags hang in a row, gold, their eyeholes cut, turning a little on their pins in the wind off the lake. LARGE is on the fourth one, in Celeste’s marker.
body.else: Behind them on the clothesline, between two of Celeste’s sheets, the bags hang in a row, gold, their eyeholes cut, turning a little on their pins in the wind off the lake, one of them too big for anybody but Tony.

body: The back screen door goes. Lena comes down the steps with a laundry basket on her hip and his pen behind her ear, and crosses the yard behind the sawhorses to the shed, where the washer is. She says nothing to either of them. Tony watches her cross. When she’s at the shed he looks at Jack, who has stopped with the drill against the wood, and then he picks up the next screw.
In the kitchen window over the sink Celeste is drying a pot she has been drying for some time.
When the last screw is in, Tony stands the ladder up in the grass and climbs it to test the box, all of him, and the ladder takes the news hard. He stops on the third step. “Hold it.”
Jack takes the rails.
“Hold it like you mean it, son.”

He holds it like he means it. Tony goes the rest of the way and turns round and sits in the gold box with his knees up round his ears, and bounces, twice, while Clovis says the Lord’s name in a tone that is not a prayer. Up there, with his forearms on the bar and Dupre Street under him, Tony looks down at Jack’s hands on his ladder.
“Your daddy,” Tony says. “He build things?”

response: “The first one he built the year I was born. The second one he built right.”
Tony nods down at that, slowly.
“Twice is how you know it’s a porch,” Tony says, and comes down.

choices.text: “He used to. He’s waiting on Lordstown.”
response: Up in the box Tony finds a screw head standing proud of the plywood, and takes the screwdriver out of his back pocket and drives it home by hand, and for the length of a screw going in there’s only that, and WWL arguing about Endymion’s route on the boil pot.
“Till they call him back,” Tony says, “you tell him come down here. There’s always a ladder.”
He puts the screwdriver back in his pocket and stays up there a minute, looking down Dupre Street toward Orleans.

choices.text: “He built a Cobalt. On a line. Mostly.”
response: Clovis laughs into his coffee, a bark that sends Aints III out from under the picnic table to see.
Tony doesn’t. He looks down at Jack from the gold box.
“Mostly’s a car,” Tony says, and comes down.

s07.slug: FRIDAY · 3:40 PM · THE KITCHEN — CHECK YES OR NO
body: The afternoon comes in low over the sink and lies across the oilcloth in a long yellow bar with pecan shells in it. The front door bangs off its stop, and the twins come down the hall in their school polos with their backpacks and a brown paper lunch sack each, folded over at the top and stapled, with JOSIE B. and JUDE B. on them in a teacher’s red marker. Their school had its party at two. They are thirteen, and above it, and they would like the kitchen to know.
Josie upends hers on the oilcloth anyway, across the table from where Jack is shelling the pecans Celeste gave him, and sorts, and grades, aloud.

“Hannah Montana. Hannah Montana. SpongeBob — that’s a boy who didn’t try. Pencil with hearts on it from Brianna, that’s a bribe, Brianna wants my science notes.” She holds one up at arm’s length: a Jonas Brother, with a sucker taped through his chest. “Brandon Landry.” It goes on a pile by itself. “Brandon knows what he did.” A Bella and Edward, folded over a Tootsie Roll. “Team Edward, from Kaitlyn. Kaitlyn and I are done.” She looks up at Jack across the pile. “Did *you* get any?”
“I’m in college.”
“So no,” Josie says, and goes back to grading.

At the stove Celeste keeps her back to all of it, with the hood fan going over a pot of something with shrimp in it, and lifts the lid, and looks, and puts it back, which is as much as she will say about valentines.

body.text: Josie squares the Hannah Montanas without looking up. “Mémère asked me who’s in Canada,” she says. “*I* didn’t tell her.”
“I know,” Jack says. “I did.”

body: She sweeps the pile back into the sack, takes a pen out of the jar by the phone, and goes off up the hall with it.

Jude hasn’t upended anything. His sack sits at his elbow with the staple still in it and JUDE B. facing the wall. Jude is the quiet one, the one who eats his rice off the back of his fork and says *Who dat* at the television and nothing else. He waits until the door at the end of the hall has closed, and then he unbuttons the second button of his polo and takes out a piece of red construction paper folded twice, and unfolds it on the oilcloth, and turns it round so it faces Jack.

body.title: Red construction paper, folded twice
body.text:
Will you be mine?
Check yes or no
☐ YES   ☐ NO
— Destiny T.

body: The print is round and careful, a girl’s, and somebody has gone over the boxes twice with a ruler.

“Destiny Thibodeaux,” Jude says. “Homeroom. She sits in front of me.” He looks at the refrigerator, where Celeste’s calendar has ENDYMION written across Saturday in red. “Her daddy’s ladder is two down from ours.”

body.text: The only other real sentence Jude has said to him was about the dinosaur from Cabazon, at this table on Tuesday: they took its name away. This is the second.
body.else: The only other real sentence Jude has said to him was a question, whether Ohio has dinosaurs. This is the second.

body: Jude looks at the boxes and then up at Jack, with his mother’s eyes in his father’s face.
“What do you do.”
All week this house has been telling Jack where to stand, what to carry and what size he is. It’s the first time anybody in it has asked him for directions.

Behind Jude, in the hall door, where Jude can’t see her, Lena has stopped in her father’s Broussard’s Seafood sweatshirt with his pen behind her ear and her mother’s list in her hand — the secret one, written on the back of the light bill — and is reading it, and Jack can see from where he sits that she can hear every word in this kitchen.

response: Jude looks at the paper. The hood fan runs. A pecan shell goes off the edge of the table and he watches it go all the way to the linoleum.
“…Yeah.”
“Then check yes.”
Jude looks down at the two boxes like a man looking at a wire he has to cut.
“What if she was kidding?”
“Then she went to a lot of trouble with a ruler.”

choices.text: “Tell her the truth. Before the parade.”
choices.key: Jude Broussard got a valentine that said check yes or no, and asked you what you do. You told him to tell her the truth before the parade.
response: Jude takes that in with his face shut. He looks at the valentine, and back up at Jack, and puts one finger on the corner of the paper.
“What if the truth is I don’t know?”
“Then tell her that.”
In the hall doorway the list in Lena’s hand stops moving.

response: Jude considers California.
“That’s dumb,” he says.
“It is.”
Jude nods, as if the two of them have settled something about men and Ohio, and looks back down at the boxes.

body: Josie comes back down the hall for a better pen. She takes three out of the jar by the phone and tries each one on the back of her hand and keeps the third, and on her way out she sees the red paper on the oilcloth.
“Jude’s in *LOVE*,” Josie says, and is gone before he can throw anything.
Jude folds the valentine back along its two folds and puts it inside his polo, against his chest, and does the button up over it.

Lena comes in off the hall reading the list, as though she has only this minute got to the kitchen, and stops at her brother’s chair on her way to the stove. She puts her hand on top of his head, and he puts up with it.
“Check a box, *cher*,” she says. “Either one. Don’t leave her standing there.”
Jude ducks out from under her hand and takes his stapled sack and goes, not up the hall but out the back, where the gold ladder stands against the shed.

Celeste turns from the stove. She takes the list out of Lena’s fingers and writes one more line at the bottom of it against the cabinet. Over Lena’s shoulder Jack can read the end of it in Celeste’s quick hand — *lemons (6) · Baker’s · butter, LOTS* — and then the new line: *candles — 19*. Celeste folds it once and gives it back with her car keys on top, and looks at the two of them, the girl by the stove and the boy at the table with pecan dust on his hands, and drops her voice to the whisper that runs this house.
“You two. Laney’s not to see.”
From the front of the house, from the girls’ room, Laney calls out to nobody in particular that she can *hear* whispering.

s08.slug: FRIDAY · 6:30 PM → 7:50 PM · THE KITCHEN — THE TORCH
body: The big set in the front room belongs to EWTN and the rosary, and the rosary belongs to Mémère, and nobody alive in this house touches that remote. So the Winter Olympics come to Dupre Street on Celeste’s thirteen-inch, on the counter by the Magic Chef, with the government-coupon converter box on top of it like a hat and the rabbit ears pointed at the window, and NBC coming in a little green. It was supposed to be a few minutes. But the kitchen has sat down, and once a Broussard kitchen has sat down it doesn’t get up.

Tony has a chair turned backward with his arms folded on the top rail. Celeste stands, because Celeste stands, with a spoon in a pot of shrimp and okra and her eyes on the screen. Theo and Laney sit cross-legged on the linoleum with their backs to the bench, sharing a bag of Zapp’s with great concentration. Jude is on the floor by the refrigerator. Margot has the step stool, with her notebook shut on her knee. Kevin leans on the drainboard, in charge of the rabbit ears. Remy isn’t back from Baton Rouge. Lena told him on the way in, in one breath, that the doberge things are in the trunk of Celeste’s car at the curb, under a beach towel, where nobody who is turning nineteen on Sunday will look.

The piano bench came in from the front room for red beans on Monday and never went back. It stands under the kitchen window, with no back to it and room on it for two. Lena takes the end. Jack takes what’s left. Josie climbs up off the floor, because her father’s head is in the way, and wedges in on Jack’s other side, and the bench is three people wide, and the only place left for his arm is behind Lena, and then it’s around her, and her shoulder is under it.
Laney turns to say something to Lena, and turns front again without saying it, and she and Theo look at the thirteen-inch with all their might.
At the stove Celeste looks over once, and back down at her pot.
“Every opening ceremony is the same picture, Professor Lindqvist,” Theo announces to the step stool, a little too loud. “A country’s childhood, scored by somebody expensive.”
“So the thing about the luge,” Kevin says from the drainboard, “is it’s basically just —”

And the anchor comes on with the morning’s news from Whistler: the training run, the boy from Georgia, the last curve. The kitchen listens. Kevin, who was going to explain the physics of the luge, doesn’t. Celeste stops stirring and starts again.

The coverage moves on to Canada: mountains from a helicopter, a man on a dogsled, a Mountie in red with the hat. “Canada,” Margot says, “is a nation-state organized around the apology. It’s a hegemonic politeness.”
“Nice people,” Tony says. “Can’t cook a crawfish.”
On the floor Theo leans to Laney’s ear and says something, and Laney puts an elbow in his ribs without taking her eyes off Canada.

The rosary ends in the front room, and Mémère comes and stands in the doorway with her beads round her fingers to see what they’ve all deserted her for. She looks at the Mountie a long time. “*Regarde-moi donc ces chapeaux,*” she says. “*Comme des scouts.*”
“She likes the hats,” Lena says.
“She said they look like Boy Scouts,” says Josie.
“*Josie.*”

At twenty to eight the RAZR goes off against his ribs, and the little screen on the lid says SKYE (MISFIT). He takes his arm back. He gets up off the bench, past Josie’s knees, and steps over Theo, and takes it out the back door to the steps, the way he’d take any call in anybody’s kitchen. Lena’s eyes go with him to the door.

The back steps are cold through his jeans. The yard is dark to the fence, the boil pot still upside down in the side yard, and over the fence somebody else’s television has the same thing on, a little behind. It’s twenty to six in Burnaby.
“Are you near a television?” Skye says. “Tell me you’re near a television, Jack.”
She says his name the way she does at the end of things, low, leaning on it. Behind her something big goes over, chopping the air into pieces, and she waits for it to pass.

“That’s the fourth one. They keep going over toward the stadium like they’re late. I’m on an apple box behind a grip truck. That’s my entire view — a grip truck, and a strip of sky with helicopters in it. Kyle ran a cable out to a monitor on the liftgate so the crew can stop and watch, and Russ brought a lawn chair from *home*. In February. He’s been sitting in it since four like it’s the Fourth of July.”
“Save him a seat.”

“He’d save you his.” On her end a generator coughs and catches. “They’re going to stop it for him. The whole stadium.” Her voice comes in close to the phone. “Sixty thousand people are about to go quiet on cue, for a boy from Georgia. The country. I’ve never been so jealous of a director.”
He hears her breathe.
“I hate that I thought that.”

Jack looks at the shed at the bottom of the yard, and the gold ladder standing against it. “Nonna says you pray for the dead with whatever you’ve got in your hands when you hear,” he says. “She says God sorts it out after.”
“Then he’s getting an apple box and a grip truck.” She says it soft, nearly a laugh. “Okay. I’ll take that. Where are you right now?”
“Back steps. The house is inside, watching it.”
“What’s the house watching it on? Tell me exactly.”
“A thirteen-inch on the kitchen counter, next to the stove. Rabbit ears. There’s a converter box on top from the government. The lady of the house has a pot going right beside it.”

“Oh, that’s *correct*.” She sounds delighted; he can hear her sit up on the apple box. “That’s exactly how it should be seen. All that money, every camera in Canada, and the best seat in the world is next to somebody’s stew.”

body.text: “Also. The front desk called. There’s a box that says SUNDAY in capital letters. It’s been looking at me like the goose.”
“Then it’s Sunday’s.”
“*Cruel.*”
She doesn’t know about Sunday yet. He keeps it.

body: “I’m on nights through Saturday,” Skye says. “Sunday I’m sleeping until noon or Jesus, whichever’s first.”

Above his head the kitchen window is up from the bottom for the heat of the stove, and out of it come NBC, and the okra, and Tony telling Kevin something about hockey. The piano bench is right under it, on the inside. Lena is on the end of it.

choices.key: On the night the Olympics opened, Skye called from Burnaby before her shift. On the Broussards’ back steps you told her you love her.
response: “Love you back,” Skye says. “Bye, Back Steps.”
The line goes. He folds the RAZR and puts it in the Carhartt. The kitchen window above him is open, and he goes back in under it.

choices.key: On the night the Olympics opened, Skye called from Burnaby before her shift. You asked if the Mountie had lit your candle yet.
response: “I did ask,” Skye says. “On Wednesday, at the relay. He said it’s a *torch*, Jack. He said it like I’d asked to borrow his horse.”
“Did he lend you the horse?”
“He’s thinking about it. Bye, Back Steps.”
Somebody on her end yells for first team. He stays on the step after the line goes, with the phone shut in his hand, until the cold finds the back of his neck.

choices.text: “Did they let you near a torch?”
choices.key: On the night the Olympics opened, Skye called from Burnaby before her shift. You asked if they’d let her near a torch.
response: “They don’t let anybody near those,” Skye says. “They guard them like the Crown Jewels. There’s a Mountie on every corner of this city who looks like he’d arrest you for asking.”
“Did you ask?”
“I’m working up to it. Bye, Back Steps.”
Somebody on her end yells for first team. He stays on the step after the line goes, with the phone shut in his hand, until the cold finds the back of his neck.

choices.text: “I wish I could see it from where you are.”
choices.key: On the night the Olympics opened, Skye called from Burnaby before her shift. You told her you wish you could see it from where she is.
response: “You’d see a grip truck,” Skye says. “You’d love it.” Another helicopter goes over her, and she waits it out, and when it’s gone she’s closer to the phone. “I wish that too. Bye, Back Steps.”
He holds the shut phone against his knee a minute, on the step, and listens to the kitchen through the window.

body: Inside, the kitchen is as he left it, except Josie, who has spread into his half of the bench and has to be persuaded out of it with a knee. He sits down where he was.

body.text: Lena keeps her eyes on the screen when he sits down. Over the bench the window is still up from the bottom.

body: On the thirteen-inch, under the white roof of a stadium in Vancouver, the countries are coming in behind their flags, endless, Tony reading out the ones he has eaten the food of — Italy, yes; Jamaica, yes; Japan, once, in Metairie, and he’d do it again — and when Georgia comes in the team is walking with black bands on their arms. The stadium stands for the boy from Georgia. All of it gets up, every seat, and stands there quiet.

Tony takes his cap off. He takes it off to a television, in his own kitchen, and holds it against his chest with both hands, and Celeste puts her spoon down on the counter without a sound. Mémère crosses herself in the doorway. Kevin crosses himself at the drainboard, and then Laney does, right way round. The pot murmurs on its low flame. The kitchen is quiet for it.
*Eternal rest grant unto him, O Lord*, Jack says under his breath, the way Nonna says it for anybody on the news. *And let perpetual light shine upon him.*

After that, alone in all that space, k.d. lang sings “Hallelujah,” and the kitchen holds still for it. Celeste reaches over and turns the flame out under the okra. From the doorway Mémère asks what the woman is singing, and Lena tells her, “*Alléluia*, Mémère,” and Mémère nods as if that were only right. Margot has opened her notebook and isn’t writing in it. On the floor Laney has her knees pulled up and her chin on them, and Theo sits with his hands still. Lena has her hands in her lap and her eyes on the little screen, and her mouth is set, and he can see the light of it moving on her face.

It goes on a long time, the rest of the ceremony. Josie falls asleep against him and wakes up indignant. Celeste’s phone goes three times on the counter, and three times she reads it out: Remy, almost there. Tony explains curling to Margot, who has questions. The great white arms of the cauldron come up out of the floor of the stadium to meet in the middle, all but one, which never comes up. Later, out on the waterfront, Gretzky goes in the back of a truck in the rain to the other cauldron, and the kitchen cheers a man in a pickup.
“Somebody’s getting called into the office Monday,” Tony says, about the arm that didn’t come up.
“Hydraulics,” Kevin says. “Probably one bad seal.”
“Then somebody’s seal is getting called into the office Monday.”
By then his arm is around her again, and her shoulder is under it.

At half past ten Remy comes in the back door with his duffel on one shoulder and a cardboard box in both hands, from a gas station in Gonzales with the price still on the plastic wrap, and puts it on the counter in front of the Olympics.
“King cake,” Remy says. “Don’t say I never.”

Celeste cuts it with the bread knife onto paper towels, and the paper towels go round the kitchen hand to hand, purple and green and gold sugar coming off on everybody’s fingers. Mémère gets hers first, by law. Margot asks what the baby signifies, and four Broussards tell her four different things at the same time. Jack bites into his and his teeth find something that isn’t cake.
He takes it out. It’s a plastic baby, pink, the size of the end of his thumb.
“Brother-in-law got the *baby*!” Remy says.
“*Remy.*”
Theo and Laney go white as one person.
Lena licks the sugar off her thumb. “It means you buy the next one.”
“When’s the next one?”
The whole kitchen, Mémère included: “*Tomorrow.*”

Remy, unwounded, goes to the refrigerator for the milk and comes out of it with a plan. “Y’all should go see that Valentine’s movie Sunday,” he says. “The one with everybody in it. All y’all young people. Make a night of it.”
Theo and Laney, in unison, from the floor: “Absolutely not.”
Remy looks at them. Jack sets the baby down on his paper towel, face-up under the bulb, next to the sugar.

s09.slug: SATURDAY · 8:04 AM → 9:30 AM · THE PORCH SWING — AND THE FRONT DOOR
body: Dupre Street is empty. Every truck on the block spent Thursday on the Orleans Avenue neutral ground and never came home, and what’s left at eight on a Saturday is a dog asleep under a crepe myrtle, the *Times-Picayune* in its plastic sleeve at the foot of the steps, and a man three doors down hosing out a cooler with the patience of somebody washing a car he loves. The light comes down the street low and thin and finds the wet on the sidewalk. Jack has the swing and a cup of Celeste’s chicory, and the chain overhead complains every time he pushes off with his boot.
In the Carhartt the RAZR buzzes against his ribs.

body: She’s been up all night on somebody else’s schedule, in a trailer in the rain on the far side of a continent, and this is what she does with the end of it: she sends it to him. He can see her doing it, cross-legged in a canvas chair with the makeup half off and a blanket round her shoulders, typing with both thumbs and enjoying herself. He laughs, alone on a porch in Mid-City, and slops chicory on his knee, and doesn’t care, and puts the cup down on the boards so he can answer her.
