body: He is still smiling at the RAZR’s cracked hinge when the screen door bangs and Josie comes out in her father’s flip-flops for the paper, and she looks at his face going down the steps and again coming back up them, and says, “Canada,” and takes the paper inside.

At a quarter past nine a florist’s van double-parks on Dupre with its flashers going, a white Econoline with a rose painted on the side the size of a manhole cover. A kid in a fleece gets out of it with a clipboard and a long white box under his arm and comes up the walk reading the clipboard.
“Lena Broussard?”

Jack doesn’t have to call her. The screen door is already open behind him, and Lena comes out in jeans and an old Holy Rosary fish-fry sweatshirt with her hair wet from the shower, and takes the kid’s pen, and signs on the porch rail with the box laid along it beside her. A little envelope is taped to the lid. It says *Lena* on the front in a florist’s ballpoint, and only that.
She thanks the kid. She opens the envelope standing right there at the rail and reads the card. She folds the card in half and puts it in the back pocket of her jeans. Jack finishes his chicory.
The van pulls off. She lifts a corner of the lid, and a smell comes out of the box that has no business on Dupre Street in February, and she shuts it again and carries it in past him.
From the daybed in the front room, over her beads, Mémère says, “*Qui?*”
“Julian, Mémère.”
“*Ah*,” Mémère says. “*Le chanteur.*” And goes back to the third joyful mystery.

Theo and Laney are on the stairs. They have stopped halfway down, Theo with one hand on the rail and Laney one step above him in his good coat over her pajamas, and the two of them are looking at the long white box going by underneath them the way people on a levee look at weather coming in from the wrong side of the river.
Jack follows the box down the hall because his cup is empty. That’s the reason.

In the kitchen Celeste has already gone. He hears the china cabinet in the dining room open, and the little glass clink of things being moved aside, and she comes back with Grandmère’s cut-glass vase in both hands, the one that lives behind the good gravy boat, and sets it down on the drainboard by the sink. Lena didn’t ask for it. Celeste doesn’t say a word.

Lena runs the cold tap. She takes the roses out of their tissue, a dozen, red, long-stemmed, the real thing, and lays them on the drainboard in a row, and strips the bottom leaves off each stem with one pull of her thumb and forefinger, and turns each one in the light from the window and sets it back. She lays the leaves aside in a neat little pile for the coffee grounds. She doesn’t hurry and she doesn’t stop. There is no extra motion in any of it, not one, and no sigh, and no remark. Her mother takes a chicken apart like this. Her grandmother tells her beads like this. It is beautiful to watch.
Margot, at the oilcloth with her coffee and her notebook, writes one line and turns the notebook round on the table so he can read it.

body.title: Margot’s notebook, the kitchen table
body.text: Field note. The suitor sends roses. The household issues a vase. Exchange complete.

body: Kevin, beside her with a bowl of grits, reads it upside down. “Respectfully,” he says, “they’re flowers.”
In the hall doorway Josie stands with the paper under her arm, and looks at Jack, and goes on looking.

body.text: He thinks of the little outside screen on her phone lit up on this oilcloth at two in the morning — JULIAN — and her hand turning it over without opening it, by the sugar bowl, while she talked about Remy and a ladder.

body: His own went to Burnaby on Thursday.

The vase is full. Lena turns the tap down to a thread. Without taking her eyes off the roses, her hand goes out sideways along the drainboard for Celeste’s kitchen scissors, which are lying by his cup.

choices.key: Saturday morning roses came for Lena from California. You told her they were beautiful. They are, she said.
response: “They’re beautiful,” he says, and gives her the scissors.
She cuts the first stem on the slant under the thread of water and looks at it, and then at him, over her shoulder. “They are,” Lena says.

She does the other eleven the same, quick and exact, and drops them into Grandmère’s vase one at a time, and stands it in the kitchen window over the sink, where the light comes through the cut glass and lays a little scatter of it on the oilcloth by Margot’s notebook.

choices.text: “Your mother issued a vase. Exchange complete.”
choices.key: Saturday morning roses came for Lena from California. You told her her mother had issued a vase: exchange complete.
response: “Your mother issued a vase,” he says. “Exchange complete.”
Lena reaches past him for the scissors and doesn’t answer, and cuts the first stem on the slant under the water.

At the stove, without turning round, Celeste says, “That’s a *vase*, baby.” She stirs the grits. Lena cuts the second stem, and the third, and drops them in the vase, and hands him the scissors to hold.

choices.text: *Hand her the scissors when she reaches for them.*
choices.key: Saturday morning roses came for Lena from California. You handed her the scissors for the stems.
response: He picks the scissors up off the drainboard and puts the handles in her open hand.

She takes them without looking. “Thank you,” she says, and cuts the first one on the slant under the running water, and the next, and the next, until the drainboard is a row of green ends and there’s nothing left in the tissue.

s10.slug: SATURDAY · 2:45 PM · ESPLANADE AVENUE → HOLY ROSARY — THREE O’CLOCK

body.text: By a quarter to three the Orleans Avenue neutral ground has been a village for two days: pop-up canopies and folding chairs in rows facing an empty street, grills already going, a generator droning under every third oak, and ladders chained to light poles, to each other, and in one case to a shopping cart. Jack has been hauling twenty-pound bags of ice off the bed of Clovis’s truck into Tony’s coolers since noon, and his hands are red and stupid with it. He finds Celeste at the edge of the family tarp and tells her he’s walking up to Holy Rosary, and he’ll be back before the bands. “Before the *bands*,” she whispers, and goes on moving a ladder that isn’t where she left it. On the tarp Lena looks up from a knot she’s tying, and looks at him a second longer than the knot needs.
body.else: By a quarter to three Jack is walking the last two bags of ice from the Banks Street freezer to the coolers on Orleans Avenue, one on each shoulder, the long way, down Esplanade. Holy Rosary’s doors are propped open to the afternoon, and through them he can see the card in its frame by the holy water and, down the side aisle, a little light burning over the door of the box. He doesn’t owe anything he knows of. The line is short. He sets the ice on the steps where he can see it, and goes in anyway.

body.text: He walks the five blocks to Esplanade with the cold of the ice still in his hands. The oaks go over him. A man on a porch on Moss Street is stringing purple lights along his rail with a beer parked on the post, and from behind him, from Orleans Avenue, comes the generators’ one long note.

body: Holy Rosary in the afternoon is a different church from the one on Thursday: empty, high, brown, with the light coming in colored and slantwise and lying across the pews without anybody in them. The vigil candles are going in their red glasses in front of the little Lourdes grotto in the side aisle. Somebody has lit a lot of them today.

Down the same side aisle, by the dark wooden box with its two doors and its curtain, the line is four people long: two old ladies in church coats, one of them with a cane hooked over the end of the pew; a big man in a Vilma jersey with his cap in both hands; and a girl in a nursing-school fleece with a folded pamphlet she keeps opening and reading and folding up again. Over the middle door, a little bulb is lit.
Jack stands at the back of the line. The cold has gone out of his hands. The phone is in the inside pocket of the Carhartt, over his heart, where it always is.

choices.key: Saturday afternoon you walked to Holy Rosary for confession, stood at the back of Father Hébert’s line, and walked back to the neutral ground on Orleans Avenue.
response: One of the old ladies goes in under the little light, and the door shuts after her, and the line moves up a place, and Jack doesn’t move with it. After a minute he turns round and walks back up the side aisle, past the candles in their red glasses, past the card in its frame by the holy water at the edge of his eye, and out through the open doors and down the steps into the afternoon, and starts back up Esplanade toward the generators. The phone rides in his pocket all five blocks.

s10a.slug: SATURDAY · 3:05 PM · HOLY ROSARY — THE BOX
body: Father Hébert’s line moves the way his homilies do. The old lady with the cane is in and out before Jack has finished reading the Stations on the near wall; her friend takes a little longer, and comes out dabbing at her nose with a Kleenex and looking pleased with herself. The man in the Vilma jersey goes in with his cap and comes out without it and has to go back in.

Jack waits on his knees at the end of the pew nearest the box, with his forehead on his knuckles, and says the Jesus Prayer into them, over and over. *Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.* It’s the one for when he’s scared. Out on Esplanade a truck goes by with its windows down and a brass band coming out of them, and fades off toward the bayou, and the church settles back into its own quiet.

When the man in the Vilma jersey comes out the second time, cap and all, the girl in the nursing fleece leans across the pew and touches Jack’s sleeve. “Go ahead,” she says. “I’m still on the commandments.”

Inside it’s dark and close and smells of old wood and somebody’s Aqua Net. He kneels. The kneeler has a dip worn in it by eighty years of knees, and his own find it. In front of his face, a little above it, is the grille, a square of brass lattice with a cloth behind it, and behind the cloth a gray shape that is an old man leaning on his hand.
“Go ’head,” says the shape, and the Breaux Bridge is all through it.
Jack knows the voice. He shook its hand Thursday at the front doors. If the voice knows his, nothing in it lets on.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been eight days since my last confession.”

body.text: He has carried it since Wednesday at two in the morning: the attic, the streetlight across the foot of the mattress, Kevin asleep by the hatch with a rosary in his fist and Mémère asleep on her beads a floor below, and the plaid of his own shirt coming down the little screen a band at a time, and the rest of it. He hasn’t looked at it since.
He hasn’t erased it either. It is in the phone in his pocket, a few inches from the grille, with the nine before it.

He has spent the walk over trying to find something big enough to bring, and there isn’t anything. There’s the week’s small things, so he brings those: impatience with his father on the phone, a cigarette he said he wasn’t going to have, the Act of Contrition rushed on Tuesday, and that he hasn’t prayed for his girl in Canada by name since Sunday. Hébert listens to all of it like it matters.

“I have a girlfriend,” Jack says. “She’s in Canada, working. Tuesday night she sent me a picture, and Wednesday at two in the morning I opened it. In a house where I’m a guest. With everybody in it asleep.” He stops. The shape behind the cloth waits. “And —”

choices.text: “I looked at a picture I shouldn’t have. On purpose. I kept it.”
choices.key: Saturday at three you went into Father Hébert’s box at Holy Rosary and told him plainly what you’d looked at, and that you kept it.
response: “I looked at a picture I shouldn’t have,” he says. “On purpose. I kept it.”
Behind the cloth the gray shape takes its chin off its hand.
“On purpose,” Hébert says. “Good. A man who knows that much has done half my work.” A pause, while somebody out in the church drops a kneeler with a bang that goes up into the roof. “Kept it where?”
“In my phone. In my coat.” Jack puts his hand on the Carhartt without meaning to. “Here.”

choices.key: Saturday at three you went into Father Hébert’s box at Holy Rosary and told him all of it: that you love Skye, that she misses you, that you opened it because you wanted to.
response: He tells him the whole of it.

That he loves her. That her name is Skye and she’s an actress and she’s shooting a show in a trailer outside Vancouver, all night, in the rain, and she sends him texts at dawn about geese. That she sent it because she misses him. That he didn’t open it by accident and he didn’t open it to see what it was; he knew what it was, and he opened it because he wanted to. That the good between them is real — that it’s the realest thing that has happened to him in his life, maybe, and he doesn’t want to say anything in here that makes it sound like it isn’t.
It takes longer than he thought it would. Hébert doesn’t stop him.
When he’s done the old man breathes out through his nose. “All right,” Hébert says. “All of it, then.”

choices.key: Saturday at three you went into Father Hébert’s box at Holy Rosary and confessed it in a few words. He asked you one question, and you answered it.
response: “Impurity, Father,” he says. “In looking.”
Behind the cloth Hébert lets the short form stand. One question comes through the brass.
“On purpose?”
“Yes, Father.”

body.text: “You said the good is real,” Hébert says. “I believe you. That’s why I’m telling you where the door was.”

“Listen to me now. Whatever’s good between you and that girl, that’s God’s. You don’t run from it like it’s a house on fire. And the bad don’t cancel the good, *cher*, and the good don’t cancel the bad. They don’t go in the same column. A man keeps both columns all his life, and he adds them up honest.” Behind the cloth the shape shifts on its chair. “But you opened it at two in the morning in a house full of sleeping people, and you knew which column it was in.”
body.else: “Small things,” Hébert says. “Small things is where it starts, and small things is where it gets fixed. You did right to bring them.”

body.text: Osei’s columns, in a Breaux Bridge accent. Two old priests who have never met.

body: “Yes, Father.”

body.text: “That picture,” Hébert says. “You’ll look at it again?”

Jack kneels with his hands on the shelf under the grille and the phone against his chest, and tries the honest answer in his mouth before he says it, and it’s the only one there is. “I don’t know, Father.”
“Then you know what to pray about.”

body: “For your penance,” Hébert says. “A decade of the rosary for her. By her name — her Christian name, if she has one. In my church, before you leave this city.”
*Mary Catherine*, Jack thinks. *Mary Kate.*

He says the Act of Contrition, the old one, the one Nonna drilled into him at her kitchen table with the radio on — *O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended Thee* — through to the end without a stumble. Behind the cloth the gray shape lifts its hand.

“God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
There’s a creak, the old man settling back. The screen is still there, brass and cloth and dark.
“Go catch something,” Hébert says.

When Jack comes out, the girl in the nursing fleece gets up off the end of the pew with her pamphlet folded very small and goes in past him, and the door shuts behind her. He walks back up the side aisle past the candles and out through the open doors onto the steps, into Esplanade’s afternoon light, with the oaks moving over the street and the Carnival flags snapping on their poles. Five blocks off, under everything, the generators on Orleans Avenue drone. His hands aren’t cold at all.

s11.slug: SATURDAY · 4:20 PM → 7:40 PM · ORLEANS AVENUE NEAR CARROLLTON, MID-CITY — ENDYMION
body: On the tailgate of a neighbor’s Silverado a boombox the size of a suitcase is playing a song that opens on a man whistling, and three generations of the neighbor’s family are dancing to it on the grass in their coats.

body.text: Lena is crouched at the corner of the family tarp, driving a tent stake into the neutral ground with the heel of Tony’s boot. She looks up at him coming across Orleans Avenue. “Father Hébert keep you long?”
“Not long.”
“He never does.” She hits the stake again. “He’s got a parade.”

Lena is crouched at the corner of the family tarp with a tent stake and the heel of Tony’s boot. She watches him come back across Orleans Avenue, sooner than anybody comes back from Esplanade, and she doesn’t say anything at all. She holds out the loose end of the tarp to him, and he takes it, and pulls.

Lena is crouched at the corner of the family tarp with a tent stake and the heel of Tony’s boot. When he comes across Orleans Avenue with the ice she gets up and takes one of the bags off his shoulder, and hefts it, and carries it to the coolers ahead of him.

body: The Broussards have half a block of curb and the neutral ground behind it, and they have had it since Thursday, and they are not sharing. The twins’ ladder stands at the front of it with the gold box on top and the twins in the box, Josie hanging over the bar and Jude sitting back with his arms crossed, and Remy on the rungs behind them like a man on the back of a fire truck. Tess sits in a folding chair with Lucille zipped into a pink snowsuit so thick only a face comes out of it. Beau stands guard over the diaper bag. Clovis has a lawn chair, a cooler of his own, and Aints III in the quilted coat with the snaps, asleep on his feet.

body.text: Tony is standing over the big cooler with the lid up. He looks at what Jack has done to the ice in there since noon. “Who taught you that?” he says, and Jack says, “You did,” and Tony says, “Hm,” and lets the lid down.
body.else: Tony is standing over the big cooler with the lid up. He looks at what Jack has done to the ice in there since noon. “Ice, Ohio,” he says. “Like I showed you.” He moves one bag with his foot and lets the rest stand.

body: And Celeste runs it. She doesn’t raise her voice all afternoon; she doesn’t have to. She goes up and down the curb in her parka with a thermos, whispering, and wherever she has whispered, people move. Beau, Lucille’s hat. Remy — rungs, baby, not the box. Clovis, that chair goes behind the chain. The cousins from Chalmette get the end with the tree. A neighbor’s little boy is lifted off one man’s shoulders and onto another’s at a word from her, and neither man seems to know how it happened. She comes to Jack last.
“There, baby,” she whispers, and points, and he goes and stands there.

Margot is sitting on the neighbor’s tailgate beside the boombox with her knees together and her hands in her coat, watching Celeste work the curb. “It’s a matriarchy disguised as a parade,” she says to Kevin.
Celeste, who hears everything said within a block of her, does not appear to hear that. She comes by the tailgate on her next pass and hands Margot the leg of a stepladder to hold. Margot holds it.

At the corner by the barricade, in the dark blue of the NOPD with his hands on the rail, Luc stands facing the street with the rest of the detail, ten feet and a world away from his family. When Jack takes his place at the curb Luc sees him, and lifts two fingers off the rail, and puts them back.

The first floats come down from City Park a little before five, and then the light goes, and Orleans Avenue turns into something Jack doesn’t have a word for. The super floats come out of the dark under the streetlights one after another, longer than the street is wide, three decks high, lit in every color at once, every rail crowded with masked riders in satin throwing with both arms, and the crowd goes up to meet each one with its hands in the air, and the beads come down out of the night in long glittering ropes and catch on everything: the oak branches, the ladders, the twins, Aints III. One float is a Greek temple; another is a dragon. On one of them Tom and Gayle Benson ride as grand marshals, and Mid-City cheers them like a debt being paid.

Lena works the curb with her mother. Where Celeste whispers, Lena carries: she has a voice for a float that Jack has never heard her use indoors, from somewhere low, a voice that could call a shrimp boat in off the river, and she picks one rider on each float — a woman in a feathered mask on the second deck, a big man in gold satin at the back rail — and calls to that one rider and nobody else until something comes down to her. “The *cups*, cher! The purple — no, the *purple* — thank you, Lord, thank you, sir, God bless your mother.” Everything she catches goes straight up the ladder to the twins without touching her own neck. When Remy leans over the box to take a strand that was meant for Josie, Lena gives him the history of his character from his baptism forward, at full volume, without taking her eyes off the street, and the cousins from Chalmette applaud.

Jack catches nothing for three floats. On the fourth a doubloon hits him square in the cheek, and Tony laughs so hard he has to sit down on the cooler, and Clovis, who knows the first verse of everything, sings the first verse of whatever the next band is playing to Aints III, who wakes up for it. Kevin stands at the back by the tailgate with his hands in the pockets of his windbreaker, catching what lands on him and handing it to Lucille, who is eight weeks old and has no use for it. When a rider on a dragon points straight at Kevin and throws, he catches the strand left-handed without taking the other hand out of his pocket, and gives it to Tess.

Then the Saints float. He can see it coming four blocks off by the noise coming ahead of it down Orleans Avenue like a wave down a pier, and when it gets close he can see why: Will Smith, the Saints’ Will Smith, and Jonathan Vilma, and Garrett Hartley, up on the top deck under the lights, and when the people near the float see Hartley the sound they make is not like anything Jack has heard a crowd do. The curb surges forward toward the street.

Lena is behind him, and when the crowd shoves he feels her get shoved, and then her arms come round his waist from behind and lock in front of him, over the Carhartt, her hands taking hold of each other at his belt. Her chin comes down against his shoulder blade. Her weight leans into his back, and her breath is warm through the canvas, between his shoulders.
“You’re a wall,” she says into his coat. “Hold still.”

The crowd presses and lets go and presses. She doesn’t let go. He can feel her breathing against his back, fast from the shove, and then slower. The cold tip of her nose finds the back of his neck when she turns her head to watch the float go by.

From the gold box above them a plush red heart the size of a pillow comes sailing down off the Saints float, and Laney, on the neutral ground behind the ladder, catches it against her chest, and looks down at it. She turns and throws it back into the crowd behind her, overhand and hard, away from them, the way you’d throw something with the pin out. “NO hearts,” Laney says, and wipes her hands on her jeans.
Beside her, Theo has Kevin by the sleeve of his windbreaker, where his phone has been since Monday. “One picture, Tran,” Theo is saying. “Of the *float*. Swear to God. The float, Kevin.”
“No,” Kevin says.

body.text: Two ladders down, a girl in a purple beanie is up in a box seat of her own, with her father on the rungs behind her. Jude looks at her for most of the Saints float, and then climbs down out of the gold box past Remy without a word to anybody, and walks along the curb past two ladders with the best strand he has caught all night in his fist, and holds it up to her, and she takes it. He climbs back up the color of a crawfish. Josie, beside him in the box, stares straight ahead with her mouth shut tight and her eyes enormous.

Two ladders down, a girl in a purple beanie is up in a box seat of her own, with her father on the rungs behind her. Jude climbs down out of the gold box past Remy and walks along the curb to the foot of her ladder and looks up and says something nobody on earth can hear over Orleans Avenue. Destiny Thibodeaux laughs. Jude doesn’t climb back up. He stays down there at the foot of her father’s ladder for the rest of the float, with his hands in his pockets, looking at the parade.

Two ladders down, a girl in a purple beanie is up in a box seat of her own, with her father on the rungs behind her. Jude stays in the gold box with his arms crossed. He watches the parade. He watches it very hard, every float, in every direction but one, and he goes on very carefully not looking at her ladder for an hour.

body: Jack watches it from inside Lena’s arms. She watches it too: he can tell by her chin on his shoulder blade, turning when Jude turns. The Saints float goes by, and the next one comes up out of the dark behind it lit all in green, and her arms are still round him, and her hands are still holding each other at his belt.

choices.key: At Endymion, in the crowd at the curb, Lena put her arms around your waist and told you to hold still. You put your hands over hers.
response: He puts his hands over hers where they meet at his belt. They’re cold. Her hands turn under his, and take hold of them, and pull his arms in with hers, tighter, against his own stomach.
The green float goes by. Beads come down all round them and land where they land.

choices.key: At Endymion, in the crowd at the curb, Lena put her arms around your waist and told you to hold still. You held still.
response: He holds still.

He holds still for the green float, and for a band from a high school in Baton Rouge with the drum line walking backward, and for a float that is all one enormous gold horse, its riders throwing with both arms. His hands stay at his sides. Every part of him that is touching her knows exactly where she is. Behind him, against his back, her breathing has slowed right down.

choices.key: At Endymion, in the crowd at the curb, Lena put her arms around your waist and told you to hold still. You told her walls don’t catch beads. She caught one without letting go.
response: “Walls don’t catch beads,” he says.

One of her arms comes loose. The other doesn’t. She reaches round past his ribs with her free hand and plucks a long gold strand out of the air one-handed as it comes down off the green float, without moving her chin off his back, and dangles it in front of his face.
“This one does,” Lena says, and puts the arm back where it was.

s12.slug: SUNDAY · 7:00 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — TWO GRANDMOTHERS
body: The kitchen window is still more blue than gray, the yard dark to the fence and the gold ladder a shape against the shed, and the only light on in the house is the one over the stove. Everybody who comes in under it says “Morning, Laney,” and stops. Tony says it on his way to the coffee, in a voice built for the far end of a loading dock and turned down so low it seems to hurt him. Remy says it with his eyes shut and has to be steered into a chair. Josie says it; Jude nods it. Theo comes down the attic ladder already in the good coat, says it from the hall doorway like a hostage reading a statement, and sits at the far end of the oilcloth with both hands round a mug, where they can’t get him into trouble.

Laney has the corner of the table in Tony’s Saints sweatshirt, her hair in a knot, a café au lait going cold in front of her, and she takes each “Morning, Laney” with a short nod and no answer. Her pink BlackBerry lies face-up by the cup.
“Daddy called,” she says. “From Canada. Ten of seven. A four-oh-three number, I had to look it up.” She picks at an old burn in the oilcloth with her thumbnail. “Four minutes. He’s fine.”

Not one person at the table asks her a thing about it. Celeste, in her robe, puts a plate of toast at her elbow. At the stove Lena has her father’s flannel on over her pajamas and a spatula in her hand, doing eggs in Mémère’s black skillet, and she doesn’t turn round, but the spatula stops for as long as it takes Laney to say *fine*.
At half past seven Kevin’s BlackBerry goes off on the counter. He looks at the screen, turns his back on the room, and ducks his head over the drainboard.
“*Bà.* *Chúc mừng năm mới*, Bà.”

The Vietnamese comes out of him slowly, with gaps in it, and the gaps get filled with “*Dạ. Dạ*, Bà,” and once with an English word Jack catches, *parade*, and once with a laugh at himself. The voice on the other end is small and quick and doesn’t slow down for him. Kevin half turns to the kitchen. “She wants to know whose house I’m in.” He says something into the phone, and *Breaux Bridge* comes through it like a crab in a net. The small voice answers, firm. Kevin lowers the phone and looks down the table to where Mémère sits with her cup at the head of it.
“Ma’am,” he says. “My grandmother would like to speak to you.”

Mémère puts her cup down. She holds out both hands, and Kevin lays the BlackBerry in them, and she lifts it to her ear in both hands. “*Allô?*” She listens, frowning. Her eyebrows go up, and she answers in French.

And French comes back. Jack can hear it from his chair, thin and fast out of the little speaker, an old woman’s French with a different music under it from Mémère’s, clipped where Mémère’s rolls, and the two of them are off. Tony stands with the coffeepot in the air. Remy opens his eyes.
“*Les sœurs?*” Mémère says. “*À Hanoï?*”
“Nuns,” Lena says under her breath, across the stove, to Jack. “In Hanoi. They both had nuns.” The spatula hangs over the skillet. Very quietly, over the eggs, she says, “Lord have mercy.”

She gives him some of the rest, low, as it goes by: the rosary, which Kevin’s grandmother says at five and Mémère at six, and Mémère is taking that personally; the cold in California, which Mémère doesn’t believe in. Some of it she keeps. The two old women laugh together, high and dry, from opposite ends of the continent.
Then Mémère looks down the table at Kevin, from his hair to his shoes, and says into the phone, “*Ah, oui. Trop maigre.*” The small voice agrees with her at length.
“They agree about you, Kevin,” Lena says.
“What about me?”
“*Trop maigre.*”
Jack, who was *trop maigre* himself on Thursday, takes a second piece of toast in solidarity.

Kevin stands at the counter with his hands empty where the phone was, smiling. His eyes go back and forth after the French, from Mémère’s mouth to the BlackBerry and back. When his own name comes out of the middle of it, *Kévin*, the French way, he stands up straighter, and keeps smiling.

“*Bonne année, madame*,” Mémère says at last. “*Bonne année.*” She hands the phone back in both hands, and pats his hand on top of it, and he puts it to his ear. “*Dạ*, Bà.” A pause, and then, low, in English, with his back to all of them: “Love you too.”

Mémère gets herself up, on the table and then on Remy’s shoulder, and starts for the front room and the daybed, and on her way past the corner of the table she stops by Laney’s chair and puts one dry old hand on top of her head, on the knot.
“*Bonne fête, la rousse.*”
Laney opens her mouth and nothing comes out of it. She looks at Lena.
“You decreed it in English, *cher*,” Lena says, and turns the eggs.
Laney looks down at her toast. She picks up a piece and puts it down again, and keeps her eyes on it.

s13.slug: SUNDAY · 8:00 AM · OUR LADY OF THE HOLY ROSARY — WOE TO YOU WHO LAUGH NOW
body: The eight o’clock on a Carnival Sunday is fuller than Thursday and younger by a generation: Saints jerseys under good coats, a baby asleep on a shoulder in a purple knit cap, a man in a gold jester’s hat with bells on it who takes it off at the door and holds it on his knee through the Mass, very carefully, so it won’t ring. Hébert is in green. The Broussards fill the Gospel side two and a half pews deep. Mémère takes the aisle, and without anybody saying so Jack is beside her, and Lena beside him.

In the pew behind, Laney dips her fingers on the way in, crosses herself on the first try, forehead, breast, left, right, and looks along the pew for credit. Theo gives her a small grave nod. Margot gives her nothing. That is also credit.

The first reading is Jeremiah, the man who trusts in the Lord like a tree planted beside the waters, that doesn’t fear the heat when it comes and stays green, and the cantor sings the psalm about the same tree, and the man with the jester’s hat sings it too, in a big flat baritone, with his eyes shut. Hébert reads the Gospel himself. Luke: the Lord come down onto a level place with a crowd round him, and the blessings first — the poor, the hungry, *blessed are you who are now weeping, for you will laugh*. He turns it over and reads the other side. The rich, who have had their consolation. The full. And then, in the same dry voice, not leaning on it at all: “*Woe to you who laugh now, for you will grieve and weep.*” Last, the ones everybody speaks well of. Across the aisle the man looks down at the jester’s hat on his knee.

The homily is three minutes and he doesn’t raise his voice once. “It’s a week for laughing in this city, and I’m not going to stand up here and tell you different; I’ve seen Bacchus,” he says. “But Wednesday’s coming, and I’d like to see every one of you laughing people in this church Wednesday morning, because that’s the part He’s talking about.” While he talks his eyes go along the Broussard pews and over Jack and on, without stopping, the same as over everybody.
At the sign of peace Lena turns to him before he has turned to her.
“Peace be with you.”
Her hand is warm from her coat pocket. “And also with you,” he says, and on his other side Mémère pats the back of his hand and tells him *la paix*, and goes on to Tony behind her.

body.text: When the pew stands for Communion he stays on the kneeler. Mémère puts her hand on his shoulder to get herself up and into the aisle, and leaves it there while she finds her footing, and then she’s gone up, slow, without a word to him. The rest of the pew goes past his knees: Lena, and the twins, and Remy. He kneels there with the empty pew round him and watches the line go up the aisle to the old man with the ciborium, and come back. Coming back, Lena looks at him, and then at the floor of the pew as she steps past, and kneels down beside him again. No one says anything.

When the pew stands for Communion he goes up with it, behind Mémère, with Lena behind him. At the front he puts out his hands, left over the right, and Hébert lays the Host in them and says “The Body of Christ” to him in exactly the voice he used for the woman in front, and Jack says “Amen.” He steps aside and receives. Mémère, back from the rail ahead of him, has stopped in the aisle to watch him do it, and when he has, she nods, and goes on.

Kneeling after, he says Hébert’s decade on his fingers, because he has no beads: ten Hail Marys, ten fingers, and in every one of them, after *pray for us sinners*, the name her father gave her, the one Debbie didn’t. *Mary Kate.* His lips barely move. It’s too low for Lena, kneeling beside him with her forehead on her folded hands.

s13a.slug: SUNDAY · 9:10 AM · ESPLANADE AVENUE, THE WALK HOME — DUEL (1)
body: Mémère comes down the church steps into the wind and holds out both arms to either side and doesn’t check who’s there, and they’re there: Lena on her left, Jack on her right. The family strings out ahead of them along the neutral ground under the oaks, half a block of Broussards. Tony leads with his hands in his windbreaker. Remy walks backward to tell Theo something about Endymion with his arms. Laney and Margot are side by side in the grass, and Kevin has the twins. Last night is still in the gutters, go-cups and a broken strand of beads, a doubloon face-up in a crack in the sidewalk that Mémère steps on without breaking stride.
“He didn’t finish it,” Lena says, across her grandmother’s hat.
“Who didn’t?”

“Father Hébert. He got to Wednesday and stopped.” She steers Mémère round a slab the roots have heaved up. “You have to read the four of them together. Woe to the rich. Woe to the full. Woe to the laughing. Woe to the one everybody speaks well of. Four woes, Jack, one man. He’s got his money and his supper and his good time and his good name, and he doesn’t need one thing from God or from anybody. It’s the ones who need nothing.” A go-cup skitters past them in the wind, and she kicks it into the grass. “Carnival isn’t that. Carnival is the neediest thing this city does all year. You laugh this week *because* Wednesday’s coming. Every soul on that neutral ground last night knew exactly what Wednesday is. You can’t be woe’d for laughing at a wake you’re on your way to.”

It’s a good argument, built from the text up like all of hers, with a door at the far end she means to slam on him, and somewhere in the middle of it there’s a soft place he could put his foot through. He can feel himself wanting to, and wanting more than that to hear what she’d do about it. Across the hat she watches him with her chin up and the wind pulling her hair across her mouth, and waits, and doesn’t push it out of the way.
Mémère stops all three of them on the grass. She looks from one side of her to the other, from under the hat.
“*Qu’est-ce que vous avez, vous deux, à vous chicaner comme ça?*”
“The Gospel, Mémère.”
Mémère thinks that over, and starts walking again. “*Bon. Continuez.*”

choices.text: “Then they’re woes for St. Charles Avenue. That’s where we’re watching tonight.”
response: “Then they’re woes for St. Charles Avenue,” he says. “That’s where we’re watching tonight. Big houses. Balconies. Bourbon in real glasses.”

She takes it, and he sees it land, and she comes straight back at him. “We watch from the *neutral ground*, not the porch. With Clovis’s cooler and a ladder Daddy’s going to chain to Clovis’s hitch. Ask anybody on that ladder what they need. Remy alone’ll take you an hour.”

choices.text: “Ask Laney about woe. Her mother’s snowed in.”
response: “Ask Laney about woe,” he says. “Her mother’s snowed in with the Mercedes.”
Ten yards ahead on the neutral ground, without turning round, Laney says, “I *heard* that.”
Lena keeps her eyes front. “She’s nineteen today, Jack. She’s not deaf.”

choices.text: “Everybody in that church this morning needed something.”
response: He thinks of the man with the jester’s hat on his knee, holding it still, and the baby asleep in the purple cap, and the old women at the rail with their hands out.
“Everybody in that church this morning needed something,” he says.
Lena takes a step before she answers, and another. “Yes,” she says. “Everybody did.”

choices.text: “Read the *now*. Woe to you who think now is all there is.”
response: “Read the *now*,” he says. “Woe to you who laugh *now* — who think now is all there is. Who think they’ve already been paid.”
She looks at him sideways across her grandmother’s hat, a long look, with the oaks going by over her head, and for half a block she has nothing to say to that.

s13b.slug: SUNDAY · 9:20 AM · ESPLANADE AT DUPRE — DUEL (2)
body: At the corner of Dupre they have to wait on a pickup with somebody else’s ladder roped in its bed, white, a child’s seat bolted on top, headed uptown already for a parade that won’t roll till dark. Mémère glares it past. Lena uses the time.

“And you want precedent,” she says, “I’ve got precedent. Thomas. *Summa*, second part of the second part, question one-sixty-eight, article two: play is the soul’s rest, the same as sleep is the body’s, and the man who does it well has a virtue. It has a name. *Eutrapelia.* Aristotle’s word. A well-turned wit. Article four: the man who won’t play, and won’t let anybody else, is a burden on everybody round him, and he’s in sin.” The pickup clears the corner. She starts her grandmother across. “That’s Thomas. Not me. Thomas had a *good time*.”
“Thomas also says it has to suit the time and the place. Same article. You don’t tell jokes at a deathbed.”
“And this is the time and this is the place. That’s what Carnival *is*, Jack. It’s a whole city agreeing on when.” She gets Mémère up the far curb.

“And Luke answers his own woe in the same breath. *Blessed are you who are now weeping, for you will laugh.* Same laughing. Same people.” She looks up at him past the hat. “They just get the order right.”

choices.text: “Then why’s the woe in there at all?”
response: “Then why’s the woe in there at all?” he says. “If it’s the same people. He could’ve stopped at blessed.”
“Because people skip to the laughing.” She says it ahead of them, not to him, and doesn’t give him the point, and doesn’t take it either.

choices.text: “Thomas never saw Remy on a ladder.”
response: “Thomas never saw Remy on a ladder.”

“Thomas would’ve *held* the ladder,” Lena says, with complete conviction. “Thomas would’ve held it with one hand and had a plate of something in the other, and Remy would have gotten every throw on the float.”
“Then we’re the same people,” he says.
Lena stops on the sidewalk. It lasts the length of one step, her hand tight on her grandmother’s sleeve, her face turned up to his across the hat.

choices.text: “Weeping first. Laughing after. It’s a promise about order.”
response: “Weeping first,” he says. “Laughing after. It’s a promise about the order things come in.”
“That’s what I *said*.”
“I know. I’m agreeing with you better.”
She opens her mouth to answer that, and shuts it.

s13c.slug: SUNDAY · 9:30 AM · THE GATE ON DUPRE STREET — MÉMÈRE’S WORD
body: At the gate in the chain-link Mémère lets go of both of them to work the latch herself, because it sticks and she knows how. With the gate open and her hand on it she turns round and looks them over, him and then her, the way she looked at the Mountie on Friday, and says what she thinks.

body.text: “*Vous avez raison, tous les deux.*”
“She says we’re both right,” Lena says.
“Is that what she said?”
“It’s what she *meant*.”
She points one finger at Jack. “*Il a raison.*”
Lena becomes very interested in the camellia by the porch steps. She doesn’t translate it, and that translates it fine, and Mémère, satisfied, starts up the steps.
She laughs at him, out of the bottom of her chest, and reaches up and pats his face twice with her dry hand. “*Il est drôle, lui.*”
“She says you’re funny,” Lena says.
“Is that good?”
“In French it’s a diagnosis.”
She points one finger at her granddaughter. “*Elle a raison.*”
“She says I’m right,” Lena says, before the finger is down.

body: The screen door bangs, and Kevin is in the hall behind it with his mother’s keys already off the hook and round his finger. “Ten minutes,” he says. “It’s an hour to the East with the bridge.”

s14.slug: SUNDAY · 10:40 AM · MARY QUEEN OF VIETNAM, NEW ORLEANS EAST — TẾT
body: The gunpowder gets there first. It hangs low over the church grounds, sharp and burnt and faintly sweet, a morning’s worth of it, with charcoal and fish sauce and frying dough threaded through, and the red paper of spent firecrackers lies in drifts along the curbs like leaves in some other country’s October.

It was forty minutes, not an hour. Kevin drove his mother’s Odyssey with both hands, the La Vang rosary swinging under the mirror, Margot in the front with the map she didn’t need, Jack and Lena in the middle row, Theo and Laney in the way-back. I-10 East went up over the high rise, and from the top of it the Industrial Canal lay a long way down, gray and straight as a ruler, the barges nosed in along it. Past the canal, the East: a shopping mall beside the interstate with its lot empty and the weeds up through the stripes; a church with scaffolding still up its steeple; a roller coaster standing out of a field by the exit ramp, with nothing on it and no one under it. Kevin taught the van to say *Chúc mừng năm mới* and how to bow to an elder. “From the waist,” he said into the mirror. “Not the neck. The neck is a cervical bow. I need lumbar.” Lena got the greeting on her second try. Laney never got it at all and was radiant about it.

The festival fills the grounds between the church and the parish hall, and it’s red from one end to the other: red banners lettered in gold, red lanterns strung over the walks, red envelopes, red dresses. Families in *áo dài* with parkas over them stand in knots by the folding tables, and the old men sit at card tables under a tent with their hats on, drinking tea out of glass cups and not hurrying anybody. At the back of it all the church stands with its doors propped open, and the late Mass is letting out down the steps in a slow tide of hats and strollers and old women on their sons’ arms, into the smoke. Over all of it a loudspeaker on a pole plays an old song, a chorus of voices raising a glass, scratchy and enormous. On the cinderblock wall of the parish hall, behind the food tables, the old line runs at the height of a man’s shoulder, faint and brown, and somebody has hung the biggest red banner of the lot straight across it.

Theo stops to stare at the lion. It’s two men under a gold-and-red body with fur at the edges and a great square painted head that blinks its eyelids and snaps its jaw, dancing to a drum and a cymbal down the walk toward the church. “Picture it,” Theo says. “A dragon —”
“Lion,” says Kevin.
“A lion, then. With a dragon’s publicist.”
There are strings of firecrackers hung from bamboo poles along the walk, long red ropes of them taller than Tony, and a man in a Saints cap goes down the line with a punk.

Then the poles go off. A wall of noise comes at them down the walk, a crackling roar with no gaps in it, red paper blowing out of it in flakes and smoke rolling up white and blue until Jack can’t see the church, or the lion, or Theo a yard off, and the drum goes on somewhere inside it all and the children scream with joy. And in the middle of it Lena’s hand finds his.

He doesn’t see her reach for it. It’s just there, her fingers through his, cold from the morning, holding hard. His close on it. The smoke comes round them both, and the lion comes through it snapping its jaw, close enough to touch, and past, and on toward the church doors with its drummer behind it. The last string sputters and quits. The smoke thins to haze, and the haze to a smell, and the walk comes back with red paper all over it, and her hand is still in his. Laney, ten feet off, who has been watching them instead of where she’s going, walks face-first into a bamboo pole.
“I’m *fine*,” Laney says, to the pole.
Lena lets go of him and goes to see about her. Jack’s hand is still warm.

Under the old men’s tent an auntie in a quilted vest and a gold áo dài is giving out red envelopes from a basket to the young and the unmarried, two hands for each, and Kevin herds them into line. Margot accepts hers like a grant. Theo bows too low and gets a laugh. Laney gets hers, and something said over it in Vietnamese, and then a second envelope on top of the first, and Vy — sixteen, in a Brees jersey down to her knees and eyebrows like a judge’s, who has attached herself to them somewhere between the food tables and the lion — translates without being asked. “That one’s for your birthday.”

body.title: A red envelope, printed in gold
body.text:
CHÚC MỪNG NĂM MỚI
AN KHANG THỊNH VƯỢNG

body: Laney looks at Kevin. Kevin is counting his own envelopes.
“They give you *money*?” Laney says. “On *purpose*?”

The auntie looks past her at Jack and Lena, who are standing in line together, close enough that their sleeves touch, and she says something to the other aunties at the table, and the aunties’ table laughs.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, “I’m not translating that.”
Vy is. She has been waiting for this since the lion. “She says next year *you two* give.” And when Jack looks at her: “Married people give envelopes.”
“We’re not —” Lena says.
“— married,” Jack says.
Vy turns and consults the auntie, who answers at some length. Vy turns back.
“She says *yet*.”

Laney’s mouth opens and shuts. Theo informs nobody in particular that the lion is two men from Gretna and they are union. Lena tucks her envelope inside her jacket, against her ribs. She doesn’t look at Jack. Her shoulder, in the line, is still against his.

s14a.slug: SUNDAY · 11:40 AM → 1:20 PM · THE PHẠM HOUSE, VILLAGE DE L’EST
body: The Phạm house is three streets from the church, a brick ranch on a slab with a garden out back where the yard ought to be, all raised beds and bamboo stakes and winter greens, and every pair of shoes the family owns lined up on the carport. Inside it’s warm and loud, and every window is fogged. In the front room, high on the wall, the Sacred Heart and Our Lady of La Vang stand over a shelf of the family’s dead in black-and-white and hand-tinted photographs, with oranges and a pomelo set out before them and incense going in a bowl of sand, and Mr. Phạm, who walked them over from the church, bows to it before he says hello to anybody living, and so does Kevin.

Mr. Phạm Văn Lộc is small and square, in a cardigan buttoned wrong, with Kevin’s two hands in both of his, and he says something to Kevin that goes on for some time. Vy translates it for the rest of them. “He says he and Kevin’s dad were on Pulau Bidong together in 1979, and Kevin’s dad gave him half a fish, and he’s been trying to pay it back for thirty years.” Kevin says something back in Vietnamese, and Mr. Phạm laughs and won’t let go of his hands.

The table is two tables pushed end to end with a third card table at the foot, and it isn’t enough. Grandparents, aunties, uncles, cousins in Saints jerseys, a baby passed hand to hand down one side like a collection plate, and food on every square inch: the bánh chưng cut in squares, pork braised dark with eggs in it, pickled leeks, a plate of watermelon seeds dyed red that the old men crack with their front teeth. Theo has been put at the card table at the foot with the cousins and is teaching a seven-year-old in a Reggie Bush jersey to say *Dude, where’s my car?* with feeling. Laney sits between two aunties who have somehow found out it’s her birthday, and who feed her off their own chopsticks; across the table Kevin is very busy with his rice. Lena bows to the grandparents at the head and gives them *Chúc mừng năm mới* the way Kevin taught it, and the grandfather says something that makes the aunties nod at her.

The aunties seat Kevin in the middle of the long side, where the good son goes, and they seat Margot right next to him, and Jack watches them decide, across the platters and in no language he has, that the tall blonde girl beside Kevin is Kevin’s girlfriend. One of them pats Margot’s arm. One of them puts the best of the pork in front of her. Margot lets them. She eats the pork.
On her way past him to the kitchen with a stack of plates she offered to carry, she stops behind Jack’s chair long enough to say, very low, “I’m here as a cultural observer,” and goes on.

Kevin has on the smile he uses for photographs, the one from the floor picture on the Delgado bulletin board, and he keeps it on through the soup and the rice and the pork and the questions, all of them, in two languages. When Margot comes back she sits down and puts one hand on the back of his chair, and leaves it there. Jack sees the smile, and the hand on the chair, and eats his rice.
An auntie in a sweater with a sequined tiger on it loads his plate, and when he has eaten that she loads it again, with a look at his wrists, and says nothing about it to anybody.

When the fruit comes, Mr. Phạm’s mother is brought from the head of the table to the middle of it on two grandsons’ arms. She is ninety-one, Vy says, and the size of a twelve-year-old, in a black velvet hat with a jet pin in it and a brown cardigan over her áo dài, and she has a red envelope ready in her hands. She chooses Jack. She holds it out to him in both hands, and when he takes it in both of his she keeps hold of her end and looks up at him and asks him something in a voice like paper.
“She asks,” Vy says, “what you wish for, for the new year.”
The table goes quieter, the near end of it. Lena has stopped peeling her orange.

response: “That my brother comes home,” he says.

Vy says it in Vietnamese. The old woman listens with her head on one side. She nods, slowly, as if that were the only correct answer and she’d been waiting all morning for somebody to give it, and lets go of her end of the envelope, and says something to him.
“She says then it will be a good year for your mother.”
Across the table Lena puts the orange down on her plate, half peeled, and doesn’t pick it up again for a while.

choices.key: At Tết in New Orleans East, Mr. Phạm’s mother gave you a red envelope and asked your wish for the year. To say what you mean, you told her.
response: “To say what I mean,” he says.
Vy says it in Vietnamese. The old woman listens, and then she doesn’t answer him at all. She turns her head under the velvet hat and looks across the table at Lena, and says something short.
Vy opens her mouth, and shuts it, and goes on shutting it.
“What’d she say?” Jack says.
“Nope,” says Vy, delighted, and reaches for the watermelon seeds. Across the table Lena has gone back to her orange, and is peeling it very thoroughly.

response: “A Browns season,” he says.
Vy translates it, or tries to. The old woman frowns and asks a question back.
“She asks what is a Browns.”
“Exactly,” Jack says.

Vy tells her something that takes longer than it should, and the old woman looks at him with deep pity, lets go of the envelope, and pats his hand twice, the way you’d pat a man who has told you the name of his illness. At the foot of the table Theo has his face in his napkin.

choices.key: At Tết in New Orleans East, Mr. Phạm’s mother gave you a red envelope. You bowed the way Kevin taught you and said the greeting right, and she gave you a second envelope.
response: He doesn’t answer the question. He stands up out of his folding chair, puts the envelope between his palms, and bows from the waist, lumbar, not cervical, and says it the way Kevin taught it in the van: “*Chúc mừng năm mới*, Bà.”
The old woman laughs, a high delighted crackle. She says something to the table that makes the aunties clap, digs in the pocket of the cardigan, and gives him a second envelope on top of the first.
Across the table Kevin keeps the photograph smile and passes Margot the pickled leeks.

s15.slug: SUNDAY · 1:40 PM · I-10 WEST, THE HIGH RISE — WHAT YOU SAID ON ESPLANADE
body: The radio has been off since the Phạms’ street went out of sight behind them. There’s only the engine and the tires, and the heater going, and the van leaning into the climb.

They are all of them full past sense. The aunties sent them out the door with foil packets in every hand, and the foil crackles in laps all over the van. Margot has her head against the passenger window and her eyes shut; she’s asleep, or giving a careful performance of a woman asleep. Jack sits in the middle row with the red envelopes stiff in the breast pocket of the Carhartt, against the tin.
Lena, in the other chair, leans across the gap between the chairs, and puts her head down on his shoulder.

She isn’t asleep. Her eyes are open; he can feel her lashes go against the canvas when she blinks. She hasn’t said she’s tired, or cold, or anything. She just puts her head there, the weight of it settling into the hollow under his collarbone, and keeps it there, and looks out the windshield past Kevin’s headrest at the high rise coming up ahead of them, gray and steep, the guardrail climbing.

In the way-back Laney has both hands clapped over her mouth. Beside her Theo has got the *Picayune* parade schedule out of his coat and is reading Bacchus’s float order under his breath, float by float, to nobody. Kevin drives with both hands.

body.text: The tires go up the grade with a long rising hum. He can feel her breathing against his arm, slower than his own, and makes his slow down to it. The van climbs. Her hair is under his jaw and smells of gunpowder still, and of the Phạms’ kitchen, and under that of her. Her ear is cold where it touches his neck. The medal has come out of her collar and lies on the canvas over his arm, on its mended chain, catching the white light off the windshield when the van shifts lanes. Her hand lies on her own knee, near his. He doesn’t move. He wants to put his face down into her hair, and he sits in a moving van full of their friends with his hands on his own legs and feels the want go all through him, steady as the engine, and lets it, and sits still. Up front, Margot doesn’t stir.

body: He puts his mouth near the top of her head, and says it low, where only she can get it.
“What you said on Esplanade. Sunday night.”
She doesn’t lift her head.
“I was asleep.”
“You weren’t.”

They come up over the top of the high rise. Out her window the Industrial Canal lies down there a long way, gray and flat, with a tug pushing something up it slow, and the low city laid out past it to the river under a white sky, the steeples and the water towers and the Superdome sitting on the far edge of it like a dropped cake pan. It goes by. Her head doesn’t move.
“…What did I say?”
Her hair moves against his jaw when she says it. In the way-back nothing makes a sound at all.

choices.key: In the van on I-10, with Lena’s head on your shoulder, you asked about what she said on Esplanade the night of the Super Bowl. She asked what she’d said. You told her: that her mother would kill you.
response: “You said Mama’ll kill me.”
Against his shoulder he can feel her mouth move. “She will.” Her weight settles a little further into him. “She’ll send you for ice first.”
Her head stays, all the way down the far side of the bridge, and the city comes up to meet them roof by roof, blue tarp and slate and tin, and she watches it come with her cheek on his coat.

choices.key: In the van on I-10, with Lena’s head on your shoulder, you asked about what she said on Esplanade the night of the Super Bowl. She asked what she’d said. You told her she’d said she wanted you here. I did, she said.
response: “That you wanted me here.”

The van starts down the far side of the bridge. The canal goes out of her window and the roofs come up, blue tarp on one of them still, a cemetery all white tombs in rows like a town for dolls. She doesn’t move.
“I did,” she says.

She says it with her cheek on his shoulder, and it’s all there is in the van. Whatever would come after that doesn’t come, from her or from him. Her head stays down on his shoulder, and her hand on her knee, and the van runs down off the high rise into the city with the two of them sitting just like that.

choices.key: In the van on I-10, with Lena’s head on your shoulder, you asked about what she said on Esplanade the night of the Super Bowl. She asked what she’d said. You told her it was nothing, and to go back to sleep.
response: “Nothing,” he says. “Go back to sleep.”
“Okay.”

She doesn’t sleep. Her eyes stay open on the windshield, on the city coming up and the white tombs along the interstate. After a while her hand comes up off her knee and finds his sleeve, a fold of the Carhartt at the wrist, and takes hold of it, and keeps it. He lets her. He looks out his own window at New Orleans going by and keeps his arm exactly where it is, so as not to lose it.

s15a.slug: SUNDAY · 2:04 PM · N. DUPRE STREET, THE CURB
body: Kevin brings the Odyssey in at the curb, its back window still lettered WHO DAT, and puts it in park, and turns off the engine. He sits with his hands on the wheel.
Lena lifts her head when the engine stops, and not before. She sits up in her own chair and pulls her hair back over one shoulder, and looks out her window at the house.
Laney is out of the way-back before the side door has finished sliding open, past Theo’s knees and between the middle chairs, onto the sidewalk and up the front steps.
In the quiet the RAZR goes off in Jack’s coat.

s16.slug: SUNDAY · 4:30 PM → 5:30 PM · ST. CHARLES AVENUE NEAR NAPOLEON — THE FIRST THING
body: Every parade of the week has come down St. Charles Avenue, and the live oaks have kept a little of each. Beads hang in the branches as far up toward Napoleon and as far down toward town as Jack can see: purple and green and gold, a pink no tradition accounts for, strands gone gray from a year of weather and strands caught last night so high that nobody but the squirrels will ever get them down. The streetcar tracks lie idle down the middle of the neutral ground with the grass grown up between the ties. Clovis has backed his truck onto the grass with the tailgate down and Aints III on the tailgate in the quilted coat, and the twins’ gold ladder, which rode uptown in the truck bed, is chained to the hitch, and between the truck and the curb the Broussards have two blankets, a tarp, six folding chairs and the big cooler, and are defending them from Uptown, courteously, a yard at a time.

Uptown watches a parade in better coats. That was Lena’s ruling, delivered from the curb an hour ago, and the blankets round them bear it out: a man in a waxed jacket pouring something brown from a thermos into plastic cups, a grandmother in a camel coat with a plaid rug over her knees and a strand of purple beads over the camel, three little boys in matching corduroy fighting over one ladder. Across the avenue a big white house with columns has a speaker in its porch window, playing an old record with horns on it and a piano like a party falling down a flight of stairs, and a woman on the porch is dancing to it by herself with a drink in her hand. The light is draining out of the sky behind the oaks, and the cold is coming down to take its place.

Lena’s jean jacket has two pockets on the chest the size of playing cards, with buttons, for show. Somewhere between the truck and the curb her right hand went into the left pocket of his Carhartt, where his hand already was, and it’s there now. Her fingers were cold when they came in. They aren’t anymore. She talks across him to Tess about Lucille’s hat, which is a crocheted crawfish with antennae, and whether a crawfish is a respectful thing to put on a Catholic child for Bacchus, and in the pocket her fingers go through his to have somewhere to be.

On the tailgate beside the dog, Laney sees the pocket. She turns to Theo, and Theo has seen it too, and the two of them look up into the oaks together and study the beads up there as though they’d been assigned them for a test.
At five past five the RAZR goes off inside his coat, over his heart, against the tin and the red envelopes.

He takes his hand out of the pocket to get at it. Lena’s hand stays where it was without his for a moment, and then comes out, and goes to the cuff of her own jacket and takes hold of that instead. He steps back from the curb onto the streetcar tracks. The lid says SKYE (MISFIT).
“Happy Valentine’s Day,” he says. “I’m on St. Charles, waiting on a king.”

“I slept until noon,” says Skye. “Like a duchess. Like a cat in a window in Rome. I didn’t dream, I didn’t move, a maid came in at eleven and backed out again in terror. Happy Valentine’s Day, Jack.” The sleep is still in her voice, and under it the thing she sounds like when she has been waiting all day to dial.

body.text: “I opened it at six this morning,” she says. “In the lobby, in my coat, with the whole night still on me, standing at the front desk like a woman getting a telegram in a war picture. Because it was Sunday. I checked. The night man checked too. He went and found a calendar; he’s very thorough. And then I went upstairs and read your essay twice in my socks before I slept.”
“It’s O’Connor’s essay.”

“You sent it. That makes it yours. That’s how presents work, I looked it up.” He hears a page turn on her end. “She says it’s grace. The grandmother at the end, with her hand out. She says it right there in black and white, she practically underlines it for the slow kids in the back.” Another page. “And I still think the grandmother’s begging.” And then, slower, to herself as much as him: “Maybe begging’s allowed.”
“It’s allowed,” Jack says. “It’s about half the Psalms.”

“Don’t make it sound good. I’m trying to win.” She reads him the front of the book. She does it first as O’Connor herself, Milledgeville in every vowel, a woman who kept peacocks on principle; and then she reads it again in her own voice, slower:

“*Mary Kate. It’s still nothing.*” She doesn’t read the rest. She doesn’t need the page for it; she was there the first time he said it, on a window seat in Montecito with her knees up. “That’s still the point,” Skye says.
“*Mary Kate. The hat was the point.*” She stops there, with the rest of it unread. “It was, too,” Skye says. “You were right about the hat. I hate it.”

“*For your margins. Strike anything you want.*” She makes a noise like a cat being offered a fish. “Strike anything I want. You’ll regret that. There’s a man in here from before you, Jack, with a pencil, and I have already struck him twice. He underlined *mystery* every single time it comes up, like it was going to be on the final.”

“*I’ve read you wrong too. I’m still reading.*” She says the last of it over, not reading now: “Still reading.” And after that she doesn’t say anything. Her thumb goes along the edges of the pages; he hears it, like a deck being riffled very slowly.

“They’re right here,” she says. “They called me in for a wig fitting on my one night off, which is a crime under Canadian law, and the violets are on the makeup counter between my script and Cassie’s wig, on its head, and I have been talking to them. In front of people. I read your card to the makeup lady and she cried, but she cries at the weather, so don’t get a big head.” Something rustles close to the phone: she has picked up the pot. “White violets. In February. In Burnaby.” And then low, delighted, as if she has caught him at something: “The *hat*.”
“In case of an accident,” Jack says, “so anybody seeing you dead on the highway would know.”
“That I was a *lady*. You remembered my bit.” He hears her set the pot back down, carefully, in exactly the place it was.

“I had her down for vain, you know. Dressing for the coroner. Now I keep thinking she’s the only one in that car who planned on being found.” A pause. “That’s a kind of faith, isn’t it. How annoying.”
She reads him the card off the florist’s little envelope: “*Skye. For the hat. I’d cross the room again. Jack.*” She says the end of it over, without the card: “You’d cross the room again.”

She reads him the card: “*Skye. From the man on the porch, R-E colon* — the woman up here wrote it exactly like that, Jack, R-E colon, like you’re invoicing me — *your Colts fan.*” A pause, for timing. “The man on the porch, *regarding*. Kyle wants it framed. Kyle wants it on his headstone.”
She reads him the card: “*Skye. I miss you in daylight. J.*” And then just the last word again, slower: “*Daylight.*”

body: “Okay, news,” Skye says. “Kyle bought a Saints shirt. At a gas station in Burnaby — don’t ask me where a gas station in Burnaby got a Saints shirt, there’s an underground — and he wears it under the Colts cap now, like a man with two families. The goose has seen it. The goose has views. Russ says changing teams after the game is the kind of thing that gets a man hosed down, and he’d know. He’s the one with the hose.”
“Kyle’s welcome down here,” Jack says. “They’d have him in a gold bag by Tuesday.”

“If you were in Burnaby,” she says, and her voice goes down to where she keeps it for the dark, “I wouldn’t be on the phone. I’d have you inside the door before your coat was off, and you wouldn’t see daylight till Tuesday.” And she laughs at herself, short and caught out. “Listen to me. On the Lord’s day.”

All through the call he has heard her moving: a floor that gives under her, a drawer, a chair dragged a foot, the rustle of something. Now there’s nothing. Wherever she is, she has stopped in the middle of it and is standing still.
“Nobody sends me the first thing,” Skye says. “They send the last thing. Flowers after the premiere.”
The woman on the porch across the avenue lifts the needle and the horns stop.
“You sent the first thing.”

He stands on the streetcar tracks with the phone to his ear and his other hand cold now, and he has nothing to say back to that which is good enough, and she doesn’t make him find it. The record starts over across the street.
“Did you go up this morning?” she says.

body.text: “Not this week.”
She has knelt beside him at St. Brendan’s. He hears her sit down on whatever is nearest. “…Was it me?”
“It was me,” Jack says.
“Okay,” she says, very quietly. “Okay. Next week, then.”
“Not this week.”
“Not this week what?”
He tells her in one sentence: you don’t go up to Communion with something on you that you haven’t confessed, and he has something, and he hasn’t yet.
She takes that in. He hears her sit down. “…Was it me?”
“It was me,” Jack says.
“Okay,” she says, after a while. “Next week, then.”
“I went up.”
“Good,” Skye says, and then again, softer, to herself: “Good.”

Ten feet off, Lena is down at the curb with Josie, the two of them with their backs to him, watching the corner of Napoleon where the parade will turn. The bands haven’t come yet. The avenue is quiet enough to hear the porch speaker across it.

He folds the phone. At the curb Josie turns her head and looks at him over her shoulder. Lena goes on watching the corner of Napoleon.

“*Show* me,” Skye says, and he holds the RAZR out at arm’s length toward it. It shows her nothing. She listens to it anyway, the avenue starting to holler at a dinosaur. “I heard it,” she says when he has the phone back. “It sounded expensive. Bye, Valentine.”

The line goes. He stands on the tracks a little longer with the shut phone in his hand before he puts it away.

body: The picture comes in while the first band is still only a drum somewhere up Napoleon: *New Picture Msg*, and the RAZR takes its time with it, a stamp-sized square filling in from the top a band at a time, gray, then grain, then something he can make out if he tilts it to the streetlight.
